lessons.title: 5.1 · Planning, estimates and priorities
lessons.summary: Connect plans and criteria with effort estimates, coverage priorities, pyramids and quadrants.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: A test plan states objectives, scope, approach, resources, schedule, responsibilities and criteria. Testers contribute to release and iteration planning by identifying risks, testability concerns and effort. Entry criteria describe conditions for starting an activity; exit criteria describe conditions for completion. Estimate effort from relevant historical ratios, extrapolation, expert consensus or three-point estimates. In the three-point formula used here, E = (optimistic + 4 × most likely + pessimistic) / 6. State assumptions and uncertainty. Prioritize by risk, coverage or requirements importance, then account for dependencies and resources. A test pyramid favors many small fast checks and fewer broad slower checks. Testing quadrants organize technology/business focus and support/critiquing purpose: Q1 component checks, Q2 business-facing examples supporting work, Q3 business-facing evaluation, Q4 technology-facing quality evaluation. A related three-point uncertainty estimate is SD=(pessimistic−optimistic)/6; for O=6 and P=18 days, SD=2 days. This is distinct from expected effort.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: For O=4, M=7 and P=16 hours, E=(4+28+16)/6=8 hours. If execution of a high-risk payment test requires account setup, setup must run first. A coverage-based order starts with the case covering the most items; additional-coverage ordering then chooses cases covering the most still-uncovered items.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: An estimate is not a commitment without uncertainty. Highest priority does not override a prerequisite. Quadrants are not chronological phases or fixed test levels.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Three teams report 10, 14 and 18 hours. Can their arithmetic mean alone remove uncertainty? No: discuss assumptions. If T1 covers A,B,C; T2 covers B,C; T3 covers D,E, additional-coverage order is T1,T3,T2.

blocks.title: Connect planning, criteria and uncertainty
blocks.text: A plan communicates scope, objectives, basis, risks, approach, responsibilities, data, environments, budget and schedule. Release planning spans iterations; iteration planning refines immediate tasks. Entry criteria identify prerequisites; exit criteria identify completion expectations. Deadline expiry does not turn unmet criteria into satisfied criteria: report the gap and seek an informed decision. Estimates can use historical ratios, extrapolation, expert consensus or three points. State assumptions. The pyramid suggests many fast isolated checks and fewer broad checks; quadrants classify focus and purpose rather than sequence.

blocks.title: Worked case: estimates and prioritization
blocks.text:
A historical test/development ratio of 0.4 with 50 developer-days suggests 20 tester-days if context is comparable. With O=4, M=7, P=16 days, E=(4+4x7+16)/6=8 days and SD=(16-4)/6=2 days.
T1 covers A,B,C; T2 A,B; T3 D,E. Total coverage places T1 first. After T1, additional coverage prefers T3 because it adds two items while T2 adds none. Dependencies can constrain the execution order.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Calculate E and SD for O=3, M=6, P=15 days. T2 covers Q,R,S and is selected; T1 covers P,Q and T3 T,U. Which adds more? Classify component checks, guiding acceptance examples, user exploration and load evaluation into quadrants.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: E=(3+24+15)/6=7 days; SD=(15-3)/6=2 days. T1 adds P; T3 adds T,U, so prefer T3 for additional coverage. Component support is Q1; business examples guiding development Q2; user-focused critique Q3; technology-focused load critique Q4. These models support decisions but do not prescribe a single fixed execution sequence.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
A test plan documents means and schedule, helps meet criteria, communicates with stakeholders and shows adherence to, or deviation from, the test policy and test strategy. Content: context (scope, objectives, basis), assumptions and constraints, stakeholders, communication, risk register, test approach (levels, types, techniques, deliverables, entry and exit criteria, independence, metrics, data and environment requirements, deviations), budget and schedule.
Release planning: testers write testable stories and acceptance criteria, join risk analyses, estimate effort for stories, determine the test approach and plan release testing. Iteration planning: detailed story risk analysis, testability, breaking stories into testing tasks, estimating task effort and refining functional and non-functional aspects.
Entry criteria: available resources, available testware and an initial quality level such as passed smoke tests. Exit criteria: thoroughness measures (coverage, unresolved defects, defect density, failed tests) and yes/no criteria (planned tests run, static testing done, defects reported, regression tests automated). Running out of time or budget can be a valid exit if stakeholders accept the risk. Agile terms: Definition of Done (exit) and Definition of Ready (entry).
Estimation: decompose large tasks. Ratios: a 3:2 development-to-test ratio with 600 person-days of development gives 400. Extrapolation: for example the average of the last three iterations. Wideband Delphi: experts estimate in isolation, discuss estimates outside agreed boundaries and re-estimate until consensus; Planning Poker is a variant. Three-point: E = (a + 4m + b)/6, SD = (b - a)/6; a=6, m=9, b=18 gives 10 ± 2.
Prioritization: risk-based, coverage-based (including additional coverage) and requirements-based, adjusted for dependencies and for the availability of resources such as tools, environments or people. Test pyramid: higher layers have lower granularity, lower isolation and longer execution times (for example unit, service and UI tests). Quadrants: Q1 component and component integration tests, automated in CI; Q2 functional tests, examples, story tests, UX prototypes, API testing and simulations; Q3 exploratory, usability and user acceptance testing; Q4 smoke tests and non-functional tests except usability.

lessons.title: 5.2 · Risk management
lessons.summary: Assess project and product risks, choose mitigation and monitor remaining exposure.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: A risk is an uncertain event with possible adverse consequences. Risk level combines likelihood and impact, often by multiplication of agreed scales. Project risks threaten delivery, such as staff loss or unavailable environments. Product risks threaten product quality, such as wrong payments or insecure access. Product risk analysis identifies and assesses risks; it guides scope, effort, techniques, coverage and priority. Possible responses include mitigation, acceptance, transfer and contingency planning. Testing reduces uncertainty and can reduce the probability of delivering defects, but residual risk remains and must be communicated.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Risk A has likelihood 2 and impact 5, level 10; risk B has likelihood 4 and impact 2, level 8. Under that model A ranks higher. Delayed environment delivery is a project risk; incorrect transaction totals are a product risk. More thorough checks may be allocated to totals because financial consequences are severe.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Risk likelihood is not impact. Multiplying ordinal ratings is a prioritization convention, not a precise probability of loss. A passing suite does not erase residual risk.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A release contains an untested authentication change. What should a status report include? The affected risk, missing evidence, consequences and proposed actions so the decision-maker can make an informed acceptance or mitigation decision.

blocks.title: Use risk assessment to choose actions
blocks.text: Identification lists adverse events; assessment considers likelihood, impact and priority. Project risks threaten schedule, resources or scope; product risks threaten delivered quality. Quantitative levels can multiply likelihood and impact; qualitative matrices use agreed categories. Ordinal scores are not calibrated probabilities. Risk-based testing uses the analysis to select levels, types, techniques, coverage and effort. Mitigation implements actions; monitoring checks their effectiveness and emerging exposure. Acceptance, transfer and contingency planning are other responses.

blocks.title: Worked case: invoice priorities
blocks.text: On a 1-5 scale, incorrect tax has likelihood 3 and impact 5, score 15; cosmetic alignment has 4 and 1, score 4. Prioritize tax-rule review, boundaries, combinations and regression. Separately, an unavailable test service threatens schedule: arrange controlled substitution and later real-interface evidence. Report remaining financial risk if needed data cannot be tested. These scores support comparison, not exact forecasts of failure rates.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Authorization checks and tests mitigate invoice-access risk. What evidence should be monitored, and why is a falling overall defect count insufficient?

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Monitor relevant role/ownership coverage, denied-access outcomes, unresolved findings and new paths introduced by changes. Reassess the risk using this evidence. A falling count can reflect less testing or fewer cosmetic findings; it does not establish effective mitigation of unauthorized access.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
Risk management has two parts: risk analysis (identification and assessment) and risk control (mitigation and monitoring). Risk-based testing selects, prioritizes and manages test activities from them. Risk likelihood is a probability greater than zero and less than one; impact is the harm.
Project risks: organizational (late deliveries, inaccurate estimates, cost cutting), people (skills, conflicts, communication, staff shortage), technical (scope creep, poor tool support) and supplier (third-party delivery failure, bankruptcy). They affect schedule, budget or scope. Product risks relate to quality characteristics: missing or wrong functionality, incorrect calculations, runtime errors, poor architecture, inefficient algorithms, slow response, poor user experience, security vulnerabilities. Possible consequences: user dissatisfaction, lost revenue, trust or reputation, damage to third parties, high maintenance costs, help desk overload, criminal penalties, and in extreme cases physical damage, injury or death.
Identification uses brainstorming, workshops, interviews or cause-effect diagrams. Assessment categorizes risks, determines likelihood, impact and level, prioritizes and proposes responses, quantitatively (likelihood × impact) or qualitatively (risk matrix). Results determine test scope, levels and types, techniques and coverage, effort, prioritization, and other risk-reducing activities.
Responses: mitigation by testing, acceptance, transfer or a contingency plan. Mitigation by testing: suitably skilled testers, appropriate independence, reviews and static analysis, suitable techniques and coverage, suitable test types, and dynamic and regression testing. Monitoring checks that mitigation works, improves assessment and finds emerging risks.

lessons.title: 5.3 · Monitoring, control and communication
lessons.summary: Interpret metric denominators and report scope, blockers and consequences for decisions.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Monitor progress, coverage, defects, effort, cost and quality signals against the plan. Metrics need context: counts of executed tests say little without scope, results and risk. Control actions may change priorities, resources, schedule or scope in response to evidence. Progress reports support ongoing decisions; completion reports summarize achieved objectives, results, deviations and unresolved risks at a milestone. Tailor detail and format to the audience. Developers may need reproducible findings; managers need consequences and decisions; distributed teams benefit from clear written records in addition to discussion.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A report says 80 of 100 tests ran, with 12 failures concentrated in checkout and 20 security cases blocked by an environment issue. A manager sees release exposure, while engineers receive failure details. A control action restores the environment and brings high-risk security checks forward.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A high pass percentage can conceal missing high-risk coverage. Reports should distinguish what was tested from what remains unknown.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: The plan expects 90 executions, but 45 are complete. Identifying the deviation is monitoring; deciding to reallocate engineers is control. For a release meeting, include residual risk and decision requests rather than only raw logs.

blocks.title: Give metrics a denominator and a decision
blocks.text: Monitoring gathers progress, quality, defect, coverage, cost and risk evidence. Control changes priorities, resources, scope or schedule in response. Completion consolidates evidence and reusable testware at milestones. Progress reports support ongoing control; completion reports summarize achieved objectives, deviations and remaining issues. Tailor detail to the audience. Record build and scope, distinguish failed, blocked and unexecuted cases, and state the denominator. A developer needs reproduction evidence; a sponsor needs release implications.

blocks.title: Worked case: interpret pass rate
blocks.text: Of 120 planned cases, 80 passed, 10 failed, 20 are blocked and 10 unexecuted. Executed-case pass rate is 80/90, about 88.9%; planned-case pass percentage is 80/120, about 66.7%; execution progress is 90/120=75%. None establishes risk coverage. If blocked cases concern settlements, restore that environment or communicate the gap rather than simply running more already-covered checks.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A release has completed 95% of cases, but the remaining 5% concerns deletion and retention of personal data. Outline a useful stakeholder update.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: State the build and completed scope, the untested scenarios and consequences, the blocker, owner and expected resolution. Identify unmet exit criteria and residual risk. Request a decision about further testing or an explicit exception. A percentage without the high-impact gap can mislead stakeholders.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
Test monitoring gathers information to assess progress and exit criteria. Test control issues control directives, for example reprioritizing when a risk becomes an issue, re-evaluating entry or exit criteria after rework, adjusting the schedule for a late environment, or adding resources. Test completion happens when a level, iteration, project (completed or cancelled), release or maintenance release ends.
Metric categories: project progress (task completion, resource use, effort); test progress (implementation and environment progress, run/not run, passed/failed, execution time); product quality (availability, response time, mean time to failure); defect (number and priority found or fixed, defect density, defect detection percentage); risk (residual risk level); coverage (requirements, code); and cost (cost of testing, cost of quality).
Progress reports, produced regularly, contain the testing period, progress and notable deviations, impediments and workarounds, metrics, new and changed risks, and testing planned for the next period. Completion reports contain a summary, evaluation against the plan's objectives and exit criteria, deviations from the plan, impediments, metrics, unmitigated risks and unfixed defects, and lessons learned. Reporting within the team is frequent and informal; completion reporting follows a template and occurs once. ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3 calls progress reports test status reports.
Communication options: verbal, dashboards (CI/CD dashboards, task boards, burn-down charts), email or chat, online documentation and formal reports. Distributed teams may need more formal communication, and content should be tailored to each stakeholder.

lessons.title: 5.4 · Configuration management
lessons.summary: Preserve versioned configurations and baselines so results remain reproducible.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Configuration management identifies, versions, controls and relates items needed for reproducible testing. Relevant items include requirements, builds, tests, data, environment configuration and results. A baseline is an agreed set of versions that can be referenced consistently. Traceability plus version control helps determine which result applies to which product and test basis. Controlled changes make impact analysis and investigation more reliable.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A test result links application build 82, requirement revision 4, test suite 11 and data set 6. When a failure cannot be reproduced on build 83, the team can restore the original baseline and compare the change.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A test result detached from its build and environment may be misleading even if the test passed. Versioning source code alone does not control all test dependencies.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Which information makes a data-dependent failure reproducible? The product version, procedure, environment and data version, as well as actual and expected results. “It failed last week” is insufficient.

blocks.title: Preserve the configuration behind observations
blocks.text: Configuration management identifies and controls basis, build, cases, data, environment settings, tools and results. A baseline is an agreed configuration that can be referenced consistently. Traceability relates items; versions distinguish revisions. A result without its build and data revision may become uninterpretable after a change. Preserve controlled changes and status information to support reproduction, impact analysis and understanding which configurations have actually been evaluated.

blocks.title: Worked case: different currency totals
blocks.text: One tester uses B18 with fixture D7 and locale L2; another uses B19 with D8 and L2. Record configurations, compare changes and repeat under a shared baseline. The difference could be implementation or data. Retain earlier results as evidence of their original configuration rather than overwriting them with outcomes from the new build.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A refund screenshot says “latest build, normal data.” Name four details that support reproduction and explain how to record a run after fixture changes.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Record exact build, case revision, fixture revision and relevant environment settings such as partner-service configuration. Link the applicable requirement revision. Preserve the earlier evidence and give the new run its own configuration. Calling both “latest” obscures the relationship between changes and outcomes.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text: Configuration management identifies, controls and tracks configuration items such as test plans, strategies, conditions, cases, scripts, results, logs and reports. For a complex item such as a test environment it records the parts, their relationships and versions. An item approved for testing becomes a baseline and changes only through formal change control. New baselines record what changed, and reverting to a previous baseline reproduces earlier results. CM ensures unique identification, version control, change tracking and relationships for traceability, and unambiguous references in testware. In DevOps pipelines CM is normally automated.

lessons.title: 5.5 · Writing actionable defect reports
lessons.summary: Write actionable defect reports with reproduction evidence, impact and assessed urgency.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: A defect report should let its audience understand impact, reproduce the observation and assess next actions. Include a clear title, unique reference, reporter and date, affected product and environment, preconditions, reproducible steps, actual and expected results, supporting evidence, severity, priority and status as appropriate. Severity describes impact; priority describes urgency. Keep observations distinct from hypotheses about the cause. A reported anomaly may require investigation before it is confirmed as a defect.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Title: “Expired coupon increases order total on build 82.” Preconditions: basket total 40 and coupon expired yesterday. Steps: open checkout, enter coupon, apply. Expected: coupon rejected and total remains 40. Actual: total becomes 45. Attach the request ID and screenshot; record browser and build. This gives an investigator an actionable starting point.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A dramatic title or guessed implementation fix does not replace reproduction steps. Severity and priority may differ; a small visible issue can be urgent for a launch.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A report says “Login is bad” and includes no account state. Improve it by naming the build, account conditions, exact actions, observed message and expected result. Describe what happened before asserting a root cause.

blocks.title: Separate observations from diagnosis
blocks.text: Defect management records anomalies, analyzes and classifies them, decides actions and follows resolution status. A report may ultimately describe a product defect, test-data issue or misunderstanding. Include the object and environment, preconditions, steps, expected and actual outcomes, evidence, impact and urgency. Severity concerns consequences; priority concerns remediation timing. They can differ when a serious issue has a workaround or a small issue blocks an imminent business event. Mark suspected causes as hypotheses until supported.

blocks.title: Worked case: an actionable report
blocks.text:
Title: Refund removes the full account balance.
Build/environment: B61, staging, fixture D12, account C29.
Preconditions: payments of 40 and 70 units; balance 110.
Steps: open the 40-unit payment, choose Refund, confirm once.
Expected: refund 40, remaining balance 70.
Actual: refunded 110, remaining balance 0.
Evidence: request R88, response log, before/after screenshots.
Impact: incorrect financial amount; high severity. Priority: assessed with release owner. Status: new, awaiting triage.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Improve “Refund API is broken because the developer reused the wrong variable.” The observed refund is 300 instead of 30 on B72. How should the claimed cause be handled?

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Record payment/account state, build/environment, exact request steps, expected 30, actual 300, logs, identifiers and timestamps. Explain impact and let triage assess urgency. Treat the variable claim as a hypothesis unless investigation supports it. Reproduction and decisions should not depend on an unverified implementation diagnosis.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
Reported anomalies may turn out to be real defects or something else, such as a false positive or a change request. The defect workflow logs anomalies, analyzes and classifies them, decides a response (fix or keep as is) and closes the report; everyone must follow it, and static testing findings should be handled similarly. Objectives of defect reports: give resolvers enough information, track work product quality, and suggest process improvements.
Typical contents for dynamic testing: unique identifier; title with a short summary; date, issuing organization and author with role; test object and environment; context (test case, activity, lifecycle phase, technique, checklist or data); description for reproduction with steps, logs, dumps, screenshots or recordings; expected and actual results; severity (impact); priority to fix; status (open, deferred, duplicate, waiting to be fixed, awaiting confirmation testing, re-opened, closed, rejected); and references. Tools may fill in identifier, date, author and initial status. ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3 calls defect reports incident reports.

lessons.title: 6.1 · Tool support
lessons.summary: Match tools to activities and understand the evidence and limitations of each category.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Tools can support management, static analysis, design and implementation, execution, comparison of results, performance measurement, coverage, collaboration and delivery pipelines. Select tools for the activity and the information needed. Test-management tools organize cases, execution and reporting. Static analysis examines work products without running the software. Execution tools run checks and compare observations with expectations. Performance tools generate load and gather timing and resource evidence. Tools improve efficiency only when processes, skills and integration support their use.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: An execution harness runs service checks; a coverage tool reports unvisited branches; a performance tool creates concurrent traffic; a management tool connects cases and results to requirements. These tools answer different questions and can exchange data.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A tool does not remove the need to choose useful tests or interpret results. Recording a workflow alone does not produce a robust oracle.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Which tool fits identifying unreachable code before execution? Static analysis. Which fits organizing release coverage and linking failures to cases? Test management.

blocks.title: Select support for the activity and evidence
blocks.text: Management tools organize basis, cases, execution and defects. Static tools inspect work products; design and implementation tools assist derivation and data generation. Execution tools run checks and compare outcomes; coverage tools measure reached implementation. Non-functional tools generate load or collect runtime measurements. DevOps tools support build/delivery workflows; collaboration tools share findings. Virtual machines and containers support repeatable environments. A spreadsheet can be a test tool when used for cases or expected-result calculations. Purpose determines the useful category.

blocks.title: Worked case: message processing
blocks.text: Use tracking tools for requirement/result links, static analysis for code rules, data generation for varied messages, an execution harness for comparisons, load tools for throughput and coverage tools for reached code. A controlled substitute gives repeatable dependency behavior but does not establish correctness of the real partner interface. Record tool configuration when it affects outcomes.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Choose tool categories for unreachable code, many valid customer records, concurrent response-time measurements and linked defect status.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Static analysis supports unreachable-code investigation. Data-generation/design/implementation support supplies records. Non-functional tools support load and timings. Management or defect tracking maintains status and links. Assess fit, integration and data suitability; a tool name alone does not establish quality or adequate coverage.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text: Tool categories: test management (SDLC, requirements, tests, defects, configuration); static testing (reviews and static analysis); test design and implementation (generating test cases, data and procedures); test execution and coverage (automated execution and coverage measurement); non-functional testing (tests hard or impossible to run manually); DevOps (delivery pipeline, workflow tracking, automated builds, CI/CD); collaboration (communication); scalability and deployment standardization (virtual machines, containerization); and any other tool that assists testing. A spreadsheet is a test tool in the context of testing.

lessons.title: 6.2 · Automation benefits and risks
lessons.summary: Evaluate automation benefits, maintenance costs, pilot effort and unreliable signals.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Automation can make repeated checks faster and more consistent, reduce manual repetition, enable unattended execution and provide rapid feedback. Costs include implementation, maintenance, training and infrastructure. Risks include unrealistic expectations, poorly chosen checks, fragile dependencies, incorrect oracles, flaky results and overreliance on tool output. Use a pilot to learn integration costs and evaluate value. Preserve human investigation, exploratory work and judgment where they add evidence. Automated passing checks mean that the implemented checks passed under their conditions.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A stable API regression suite gives feedback on each commit. A recorded interface script fails after harmless layout changes and takes hours to maintain. The team moves checks to an appropriate layer and retains a smaller set of user workflow checks.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: More automated tests does not automatically mean better coverage. Maintenance effort and signal reliability belong in the business case.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A tool produces many false alarms. Is faster execution enough to justify it? No: consider investigation and maintenance costs. A useful pilot measures reliable feedback and value, not just the number of scripts generated.

blocks.title: Assess benefits and costs throughout adoption
blocks.text: Automation can reduce repetition, improve consistency, speed feedback and support difficult measurements. Initial costs include training, integration, scripts, environment and data. Continuing costs include maintenance and investigating unreliable results. Risks include unsuitable scope, fragile dependencies, flawed oracles and overconfidence in passing output. A representative pilot reveals practical benefits and costs. Investigate flaky outcomes: unreliable signals weaken release decisions even when retries become green. Human exploration and interpretation remain useful.

blocks.title: Worked case: a pilot effort estimate
blocks.text: Manual effort is two hours per run. Automation costs 20 hours initially and 0.5 hour upkeep per run; execution effort is negligible for this estimate. Manual effort after n runs is 2n; automated effort is 20+0.5n. Equality occurs at n=20/1.5, about 13.3; effort savings begin with the 14th run under these assumptions. Include infrastructure, changes and investigation when evaluating a real pilot, along with signal quality and scope.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A pipeline check passes on retry with no code change. The team proposes retrying until green. Name causes to investigate and explain why the rerun is insufficient evidence.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Investigate timing races, shared or unstable data, environment dependence and external-service behavior. Preserve the failure and rerun conditions. A green retry can hide an intermittent product defect or unreliable check; it does not explain the original observation. Improve isolation and diagnosis, and communicate uncertainty until resolved.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
Simply acquiring a tool does not guarantee success; introduction, maintenance and training take effort. Benefits: time saved on repetitive work (regression runs, re-entering data, comparing results, checking coding standards); consistency and repeatability that prevent simple human errors; more objective assessment such as coverage, and measures too complex for people; easier access to statistics, graphs and aggregated data for management and reporting; shorter execution times for earlier defect detection, faster feedback and faster time to market; and more time to design new, deeper tests.
Risks: unrealistic expectations; inaccurate estimates of the time, cost and effort to introduce a tool, maintain scripts and change the manual process; automating when manual testing is more appropriate; relying on the tool instead of critical thinking; dependency on a vendor that may go out of business, retire or sell the tool or give poor support; open-source tools that are abandoned or need frequent updates; incompatibility with the development platform; and tools that do not comply with regulatory or safety standards.

blocks.title: Syllabus references
blocks.text: CTFL syllabus v4.0.1, section 6.2 (starts on p. 59). Learning objectives: FL-6.2.1 (K1). Read the full section and the chapter keyword list alongside this lesson.

lessons.title: Final revision · Turn evidence into a study decision
lessons.summary: Review distinctions, calculations and timed-exam strategy.

blocks.title: Recall and distinguish
blocks.text: Explain testing versus debugging; error versus defect versus failure; analysis versus design versus implementation; test level versus test type; confirmation versus regression; static versus dynamic; statement versus branch coverage; entry versus exit criteria; severity versus priority; project versus product risk. Give a concrete example for each distinction rather than memorizing a label.

blocks.title: Technique checklist
blocks.text: For EP, list valid and invalid partitions before choosing representatives. For BVA, state whether two or three values are required and the input resolution. For decision tables, enumerate feasible rules before merging. For state models, count states and transitions separately. For estimation, show the formula and units. For prioritization, check dependencies and additional coverage. For defect reports, specify reproducible actions and observable expected results.

blocks.title: Timed strategy
blocks.text: Read selection counts carefully. Make one pass through straightforward items and leave time for longer application questions. Use the exact information and technique named in the question. Unanswered items score zero. Answers and explanations become available after submitting the mock or when its timer expires.

blocks.title: Review after a paper
blocks.text: For each mistake, identify the objective, explain why the chosen option failed, solve the relevant lesson example again and write a new example. Treat guesses as review targets even when correct. Use objective practice for weak areas. A repeated paper is useful revision but cannot supply fresh readiness evidence. Confirm registration and exam arrangements with your provider.

blocks.title: Explain six linked decisions
blocks.text: Choose an unfamiliar feature and explain its basis and objectives; suitable levels and types; one static evaluation; derivation and named coverage items; risk-based priority and reporting; and tool support with its limitations. Link your decisions. Duplicate-charge risk can motivate payment-rule review, retry-state checks, appropriate independence, transaction evidence and reporting of residual risk. Revisit objective lessons when you cannot explain a link.

blocks.title: Review calculations by their denominator
blocks.text: EP: exercised partitions / identified partitions. BVA: exercised coverage values / identified values for the stated variant. Decision tables: exercised feasible rules / feasible rules. Structural metrics: exercised statements or branches / identified statements or branches. Expected effort: (O+4M+P)/6; uncertainty estimate: (P-O)/6. State the model and units first. For prioritization, distinguish total coverage from additional coverage after previous selections.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a typical test objective?

options.text: Diagnosing and removing the defects that cause failures
Giving stakeholders information for informed decisions
Proving that the test object contains no remaining defects
Defining the processes the development team must follow

questions.explanation: Providing information that lets stakeholders make informed decisions is a typical test objective. Diagnosing and removing defects is debugging, testing cannot prove that no defects remain, and defining development processes is a quality-assurance concern. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.1.1 (p. 15); FL-1.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: What does the whole-team approach make a shared responsibility?

options.text: Approval of the release budget
Quality of the product
Independent system-level testing
Moderation of formal inspections

questions.explanation: In the whole-team approach everyone is responsible for quality, and any member with the necessary skills can perform any task. Moderating inspections and approving budgets remain specific roles, and independent testing is a different arrangement that may be needed in safety-critical contexts. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.2 (p. 22); FL-1.5.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: A developer investigates a failing calculation, identifies a wrong operator and repairs it. Which activity is being described?

options.text: Test monitoring
Debugging
Acceptance testing
Test analysis

questions.explanation: Debugging locates and removes a failure's cause. Analysis identifies conditions to test, monitoring compares progress with plans, and acceptance testing evaluates readiness for stakeholder use. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.1.2 (p. 16); FL-1.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A reporting product passes every written requirement but users cannot produce the report needed for their daily work. Which principle best explains the problem?

options.text: Tests wear out
Absence-of-defects fallacy
Defect clustering
Early testing saves resources

questions.explanation: Meeting specified requirements does not ensure that a product meets user needs. The stem concerns usefulness, rather than clustered defects, repeated tests or when testing begins. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.3 (p. 17); FL-1.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester studies a billing specification and identifies conditions that need checking. Which activity is the main focus?

options.text: Test implementation
Test completion
Test execution
Test analysis

questions.explanation: Analysis determines what to test from the basis. Implementation prepares procedures and environments, execution runs checks, and completion consolidates and archives outcomes. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.1 (p. 18); FL-1.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A safety-critical device and a disposable game prototype use different test approaches. What best explains this choice?

options.text: Risk, regulation and constraints shape the method
Their teams must use identical exit criteria
Their source-code languages define all testing needs
Their release dates determine the correctness of results

questions.explanation: Testing depends on context, including risk, regulation, stakeholders and resources. A language or date alone cannot determine the entire approach, and identical criteria need not suit both products. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.2 (p. 19); FL-1.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which testware is most directly created when preparing an ordered procedure for running several test cases?

options.text: A defect status summary
A test completion report
A product risk register
A test script

questions.explanation: An execution procedure or script is implementation testware. Risks support planning; completion reports summarize finished work; defect status summaries concern findings rather than executable steps. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.3 (p. 20); FL-1.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester needs to discuss a reproducible failure with its author. Which response best demonstrates constructive communication?

options.text: Delay the report until a different tester can present it
Rank the author's competence in the defect title
State a root cause before investigating the failure
Give observable outcomes and concrete steps to repeat the issue

questions.explanation: Specific observations and reproduction steps support investigation without blame. Personal criticism, unsupported diagnosis and unnecessary delay undermine useful communication. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.1 (p. 21); FL-1.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which testing practice is useful across development lifecycles?

options.text: Replace component checks with stakeholder acceptance
Wait for implementation to end before designing checks
Give component and system testing identical objectives
Review suitable draft requirements and designs early

questions.explanation: Early review can prevent downstream defects across lifecycles. Delaying all testing, replacing lower-level checks or using identical objectives at every level removes useful evidence. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.2 (p. 25); FL-2.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which approach begins with component tests before writing the corresponding implementation?

options.text: Test-driven development
Risk-based testing
Checklist-based testing
Exploratory testing

questions.explanation: TDD uses a failing component test to guide implementation and refactoring. Exploratory testing integrates learning and execution; risk-based testing prioritizes by risk; checklists guide conditions to inspect. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.3 (p. 26); FL-2.1.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: A team checks interactions between a tax-calculation component and a pricing component within one application. Which level is the primary focus?

options.text: System integration testing
Acceptance testing
Component integration testing
Component testing

questions.explanation: Component integration targets interactions among components. Component testing isolates a component; system integration concerns interactions among systems; acceptance assesses stakeholder readiness. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.1 (p. 28); FL-2.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A fix corrects the original tax-rounding failure. Why also run previously passing discount tests?

options.text: To diagnose the operator that caused the original defect
To detect unintended effects of the change
To replace confirmation testing of the repaired behavior
To establish that no defects remain in the application

questions.explanation: Regression testing checks for adverse effects on existing behavior. Diagnosis belongs to debugging; a passing suite cannot prove absence of defects, and confirmation of the fix remains useful. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.3 (p. 30); FL-2.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: An application is delivered in small increments. Which test planning response is appropriate?

options.text: Reuse the first increment's cases without reviewing changes
Limit every iteration to acceptance testing of new features
Postpone design of test cases until the final increment
Test each increment and consider regression of existing behavior

questions.explanation: Incremental development needs checks of new behavior and potentially affected existing behavior. Waiting until the end or ignoring changes loses timely feedback; one level cannot address every risk. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.1 (p. 25); FL-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A DevOps pipeline gives rapid automated feedback, but intermittently reports failures caused by unstable test data. What should the team address?

options.text: The removal of all manual investigation
The use of slower deployments as the sole quality measure
Stabilize the data and improve signal reliability
The replacement of every review with pipeline execution

questions.explanation: Unreliable feedback consumes investigation effort and reduces trust. DevOps still needs human judgment and reviews; deployment speed alone does not establish quality. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.4 (p. 26); FL-2.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which work product can be assessed through static testing before any executable application exists?

options.text: An execution of the application's binary
A live session exercising implemented checkout behavior
A draft user story
A measured production response-time trace generated by the new application

questions.explanation: A user story can be reviewed without executing the software. The other choices depend on execution or implemented behavior and describe runtime evidence or activity. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.1 (p. 33); FL-3.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: What is a benefit of early stakeholder feedback on a draft workflow?

options.text: Discovering mismatched expectations before implementation
Replacing the need for an agreed test basis
Eliminating the need to assess implemented behavior
Guaranteeing that stakeholders will never change priorities

questions.explanation: Feedback can expose misunderstanding while changes are cheaper. It neither prevents future changes nor removes dynamic testing or the need for shared expectations. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.1 (p. 35); FL-3.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A review finds contradictory fee rules before coding starts. Why does this add value?

options.text: It can prevent implementing inconsistent behavior
It proves that the future implementation has no defects
It demonstrates runtime performance under peak load
It replaces the need to test fee calculations after coding

questions.explanation: Early defect detection can avoid rework and failures downstream. A requirements review does not measure runtime performance, certify future code or replace complementary dynamic checks. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.2 (p. 33); FL-3.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Reviewers have individually recorded anomalies in a design. What is the next main review activity?

options.text: Individual review
Communication and analysis
Fixing and reporting
Review initiation

questions.explanation: After individual review, the identified anomalies are communicated and analyzed, typically in a review meeting, to decide their status, ownership and actions. Initiation and individual review come before this step, and fixing and reporting follow the analysis. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.2 (p. 35); FL-3.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO examples of black-box test derivation.

options.text: Choose a case because a similar product once failed there
Choose cases from combinations of business-rule conditions
Choose a case to execute an unvisited source-code branch
Choose inputs from specified valid and invalid age ranges
Choose a case from a checklist of common usability problems

questions.explanation: Partitions and decision tables derive from specified behavior. An unvisited branch uses internal structure, while prior failure experience motivates error guessing. A usability checklist is an experience-based source. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.1 (p. 39); FL-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: An input executes all executable statements in a function. What follows about statement coverage?

options.text: Requirements-based acceptance coverage is complete
It is 100% for that function
The business specification contains no ambiguity
That function’s false decision outcome has also run

questions.explanation: Executing all statements establishes full statement coverage. It says nothing conclusive about branch outcomes, missing requirements or correctness, so those stronger claims are unsupported. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.1 (p. 42); FL-4.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A decision has true and false outcomes. Existing tests exercise only the true outcome. What improves its branch coverage?

options.text: Repeat the true-outcome test with a new test name
Increase the number of assertions on the true path
Inspect the same execution log a second time
Add an input that takes the unvisited path

questions.explanation: The missing branch is the false outcome; executing it improves coverage. Renaming, rereading or adding assertions on an already exercised path does not execute a new branch. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 (p. 43); FL-4.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester adds cases for empty input after recalling earlier validation defects. Which technique is being used?

options.text: State transition testing
Statement testing
Error guessing
Decision table testing

questions.explanation: The choice is driven by experience with likely errors. No structural coverage, condition table or state model is used to derive the case in this scenario. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 (p. 43); FL-4.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: During a chartered session, each observation guides the tester's next experiment. Which technique best fits?

options.text: A formal inspection meeting
Exploratory testing
Three-point estimation
A fixed scripted regression run

questions.explanation: Exploratory testing combines learning, design and execution adaptively. Fixed scripts predefine the sequence; inspections review work products; estimation predicts effort rather than explores behavior. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 (p. 44); FL-4.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Business, development and testing discuss concrete examples for a user story. What is the main benefit?

options.text: A replacement for evaluation of completed functionality
A prescribed internal implementation for the agreed examples
A shared understanding of desired behavior
An implementation design sufficient to bypass reviews

questions.explanation: Collaboration clarifies needs and exposes differing assumptions. It need not dictate implementation and cannot guarantee defect-free requirements or remove later evaluation. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 (p. 45); FL-4.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A field accepts integer ages 18–65 inclusive. Values below 18 and above 65 are rejected for different reasons. Which set covers every stated equivalence partition?
questions.explanation: The three partitions are below 18, valid 18–65 and above 65. The correct set represents each. The other sets omit one or both invalid partitions; boundary coverage is not the requested measure. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: An integer quantity is accepted from 3 through 7. Which set supplies two-value boundary analysis for both edges?
questions.explanation: Two-value BVA checks each boundary and its immediate adjacent-partition neighbor: 2/3 and 7/8. Interior neighbors belong to three-value coverage; distant values skip the nearest neighbors. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A discount is granted when an account is active AND a coupon is valid. Both conditions can independently be true or false. How many feasible rules are needed in the full, unminimized decision table?
questions.explanation: Two independent Boolean conditions give 2 × 2 = 4 combinations. One permits a discount and three deny it. Counting actions alone gives two, while eight would require a third independent Boolean condition. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 (p. 41); FL-4.2.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: Model: Locked --coin→ Unlocked; Unlocked --push→ Locked; Locked --push→ Locked; Unlocked --coin→ Unlocked. Starting Locked, events coin,push have run. What is valid-transition coverage?
questions.explanation: Two of the four specified valid transitions ran: Locked→Unlocked on coin and Unlocked→Locked on push. Both states were visited, but the two self-transitions were not, so state coverage must not be substituted. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 (p. 41); FL-4.2.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: Criterion: orders totaling at least 50 receive free delivery; lower totals cost 5. Which TWO acceptance examples test the threshold correctly?

options.text: Total 50 expects delivery charge 0
Total 49.99 expects delivery charge 0
Total 50 expects delivery charge 5
Total 49.99 expects delivery charge 5
Total 50.01 expects delivery charge 5

questions.explanation: The rule includes 50 in the free-delivery class. The neighboring lower total stays in the paid class. The distractors reverse the expected results and would encode the wrong business rule. A total of 50.01 is above the threshold and should be free. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: How can a tester contribute during iteration planning?

options.text: Replace the product owner in ranking business value
Identify testability concerns and testing effort
Sign off the release on behalf of the customer
Fix the defects found in the previous iteration

questions.explanation: In iteration planning, testers analyze the risks and testability of user stories, break stories into testing tasks and estimate test effort. Ranking business value belongs to the product owner, release sign-off to stakeholders, and fixing defects is debugging. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.2 (p. 48); FL-5.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: A team needs a document defining test scope, approach, resources and completion criteria. Which testware serves that purpose?

options.text: A test execution log
An automated test result
An individual defect report
A test plan

questions.explanation: A plan describes intended testing and its organization. Logs and results capture executed work; defect reports describe anomalies rather than the overall approach and resource commitments. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.1 (p. 48); FL-5.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which activity best fits the business-facing quadrant that critiques the product (Q3)?

options.text: Load testing of service throughput
Acceptance examples guiding implementation
Exploratory usability evaluation with users
Automated component checks of an internal function

questions.explanation: Q3 evaluates the product from a business or user perspective. Component checks fit Q1, technical performance evaluation fits Q4, and implementation-guiding acceptance examples fit Q2. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.7 (p. 51); FL-5.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which is a product risk rather than a project risk?

options.text: The released application calculates interest incorrectly
The test environment arrives two weeks late
A key tester becomes unavailable during the schedule
The supplier misses a planned handover date

questions.explanation: Incorrect interest is a potential product-quality problem. Staffing, environment delivery and supplier delays threaten execution of the project and its schedule. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.2 (p. 52); FL-5.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A release manager needs to decide whether to ship. Which report content is most useful?

options.text: Detailed steps of every executed test case
The original test schedule and resource plan
Testing planned for the next reporting period
Achieved coverage, unresolved defects and residual risks

questions.explanation: A release decision needs an evaluation of quality against the exit criteria, including coverage achieved, defects not fixed and unmitigated risks. Next-period plans support ongoing control, raw test steps lack interpretation, and the original schedule does not report results. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.2 (p. 54); FL-5.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why link an execution result to build, test-suite and data-set versions?

options.text: To avoid recording actual and expected results
To remove the need for impact analysis on changes
To make the evidence reproducible and attributable
To establish that later builds have identical behavior

questions.explanation: Configuration references identify what was tested and help reproduce findings. They do not replace result details, imply unchanged later builds or remove analysis of changes. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.4 (p. 56); FL-5.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Use E=(O+4M+P)/6. An effort estimate has O=4, M=7 and P=16 hours. What is E?

options.text: 7 hours
8 hours
9 hours
12 hours

questions.explanation: Substitution gives (4+28+16)/6=48/6=8 hours. Seven uses only the most-likely value; nine is the unweighted mean; twelve does not follow the specified formula. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: For additional-coverage prioritization, T1 covers A,B,C; T2 covers B,C; T3 covers D,E. No dependencies apply. Which order is correct?
questions.explanation: T1 first adds three items. T3 next adds two still-uncovered items, while T2 adds none. Static total-coverage ordering would incorrectly place T2 second for the requested additional-coverage technique. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: A report for a checkout failure already includes build, browser, account state and steps. Which addition most directly makes the anomaly evaluable?

options.text: A proposed priority for fixing the defect
A status of awaiting confirmation testing
Expected and actual totals per the pricing rule
The reporting date and the author's role

questions.explanation: Without expected and actual results, a reader cannot judge whether the behavior is a defect. Priority, date and author are useful report fields but do not describe the failure, and awaiting confirmation testing is a status used only after a fix. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team needs to simulate concurrent users and measure response time. Which tool category is appropriate?

options.text: Performance testing tools
Configuration management tools
Test data cataloging tools
Static analysis tools

questions.explanation: Performance tools generate load and collect timing or resource evidence. Configuration tools version items, static analysis inspects work products, and catalogs organize data rather than measure behavior under load. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.1 (p. 59); FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO potential benefits of suitable test automation.

options.text: Proof that no defects remain
Rapid feedback after code changes
Elimination of test maintenance
Repeatable execution of routine checks
Independence from tool vendors and their support

questions.explanation: Automation can execute repeatable checks and provide quick feedback. Scripts and infrastructure still need maintenance, and their passing results do not prove absence of defects. Dependency on a vendor is a risk of automation, not a benefit. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.2 (p. 59); FL-6.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: How is testing commonly classified in relation to quality management?

options.text: A process-oriented, preventive form of quality assurance
A product-oriented, corrective form of quality control
A management activity that sets the quality policy
A debugging activity that removes defects from code

questions.explanation: The syllabus describes testing as a product-oriented, corrective approach and a major form of quality control. QA is process-oriented and preventive, removing defects is debugging, and setting a quality policy is not how testing is classified. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.2 (p. 17); FL-1.2.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: What is an advantage of testers, developers and business representatives working as one team?

options.text: Assigning quality ownership exclusively to the testers
Combining complementary skills to solve quality problems
Making each person equally proficient in every tool
Removing the need for any specialized test knowledge

questions.explanation: Complementary skills improve problem solving and shared understanding. Whole-team working neither gives everyone identical expertise nor removes specialization; quality remains shared. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.2 (p. 22); FL-1.5.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: A hospital system is tested before a medication workflow is released. Which reason most directly justifies the effort?

options.text: Replace the need for review of medication requirements
Transfer responsibility for medical decisions to testers
Establish that every possible input has been exercised
Reduce the chance of harmful failures reaching users

questions.explanation: Testing provides evidence and reduces delivery risk, which matters where failures may harm users. Exhaustive testing is generally infeasible, and testing does not assume clinical responsibility or replace reviews. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.1 (p. 16); FL-1.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team reviews draft requirements before coding and resolves unclear rules. Which principle does this illustrate?

options.text: Tests wear out
Defects cluster together
Early testing saves time and money
Testing shows the absence of defects

questions.explanation: Resolving problems early avoids downstream implementation and rework. The situation does not involve repeated tests or clustering, and testing cannot establish absence of defects. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.3 (p. 17); FL-1.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly links an activity to its typical testware?

options.text: Completion — new input partitions as its main output
Analysis — production deployment binaries
Planning — measured results from tests not yet executed
Execution — logs of observed outcomes

questions.explanation: Execution creates records of observations. Conditions and partitions concern analysis/design; binaries are implementation products of development; planning cannot record outcomes of future execution. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.3 (p. 20); FL-1.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A requirement changes, and links from it to cases identify which checks need revision. What benefit is being used?

options.text: Proof that all unlinked requirements are covered
Removal of the need to review the revised requirement
Impact assessment through traceability
Automatic repair of defects in the implementation

questions.explanation: Traceability enables impact analysis by relating basis and testware. Links do not perform reviews or code repairs, and absent links cannot prove coverage. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.4 (p. 20); FL-1.4.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: A small team member schedules testing and also derives cases. How should the roles be understood?

options.text: An individual can carry both responsibilities
Case derivation makes all scheduling a development role
The person must choose one role and abandon the other
Roles require different people even in a small team

questions.explanation: Roles describe responsibilities and can be combined. Scheduling is test management and derivation is technical testing; neither changes category because the same person performs it. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.5 (p. 21); FL-1.4.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: An independent tester challenges assumptions shared by the authors. What benefit does this illustrate?

options.text: Independent testers own all product quality
Independent testing makes communication unnecessary
A different perspective can reveal overlooked problems
Author-created checks lose all value once independence is added

questions.explanation: Independence can expose shared assumptions. Collaboration and shared quality responsibility still matter, and developer checks continue to provide useful evidence. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.3 (p. 22); FL-1.5.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement describes good coordination of development and testing?

options.text: Every development activity requires only production monitoring
Testers should avoid draft work products until sign-off
Testing activities should share one identical objective
Each test level has objectives suited to that level

questions.explanation: Different levels address different objects and goals. One objective for all levels loses their distinctions; production monitoring alone omits earlier evidence, and suitable drafts can be reviewed. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.2 (p. 25); FL-2.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which approach expresses expected behavior as business-readable scenarios before implementing it?

options.text: Behavior-driven development
Defect density analysis
Configuration baselining
Behavior-based coverage measurement

questions.explanation: BDD uses behavior-focused examples, often in Given/When/Then form, to guide shared understanding and development. Coverage, defect metrics and baselines serve different purposes. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.3 (p. 26); FL-2.1.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: A service is checked for response time and resource usage under peak traffic. Which type of testing is the main focus?

options.text: Non-functional testing
Confirmation testing
Functional rule testing
Static requirements review

questions.explanation: Timing and resource characteristics are non-functional qualities. Confirmation concerns a specific fix; functional testing checks what the system does; static review cannot measure live load behavior. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.2 (p. 29); FL-2.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: The application code is unchanged, but its database platform is upgraded. What testing response is appropriate?

options.text: Repeat only the confirmation tests from the last fix
Treat the upgrade as outside all testing responsibilities
Assume a previously passing result applies to the new platform
Assess affected behavior and perform maintenance testing

questions.explanation: Upgrading the operational environment triggers maintenance testing of affected behavior, including regression checks, even when application code is unchanged. Previous results on the old platform do not transfer, and old confirmation tests target a different change. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.3 (p. 31); FL-2.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A retrospective agrees an improvement but assigns no owner or follow-up. What should be added?

options.text: An actionable experiment with ownership and outcome review
A guarantee that the same issue cannot recur
A restriction to measuring individual performance
A replacement of all technical discussion with voting

questions.explanation: Retrospectives should produce useful improvements and assess their effects. Guarantees, eliminating discussion or blaming individuals do not make actions effective. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.6 (p. 28); FL-2.1.6 (K2).

questions.prompt: Reviewing acceptance examples during refinement instead of waiting for completed code is an example of what?

options.text: Delaying feedback until the release decision
Moving suitable testing earlier
Replacing system testing with code review
Moving all checks into production

questions.explanation: Shift left moves suitable activities earlier, including review of examples. It complements rather than replaces later testing and does not mean shifting work into production or postponing feedback. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.5 (p. 27); FL-2.1.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which review role primarily facilitates an effective review meeting?

options.text: Manager
Scribe
Author
Moderator

questions.explanation: The moderator facilitates communication and keeps the meeting useful. The author creates the artifact, the scribe records findings and management provides resources and support. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.3 (p. 36); FL-3.2.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which factor contributes to a successful review?

options.text: The artifact is as large as possible for every session
Findings are discouraged to protect the schedule
Participants prepare against clear objectives
The meeting evaluates the author's personal worth

questions.explanation: Preparation and clear aims support meaningful evaluation. Personal appraisal, oversized artifacts and suppressing findings undermine effectiveness and constructive feedback. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.5 (p. 37); FL-3.2.5 (K1).

questions.prompt: Select TWO accurate distinctions between static and dynamic testing.

options.text: Static review can find ambiguity in an unimplemented requirement
Dynamic testing identifies defects directly without observing execution
Dynamic testing executes software to observe behavior
Static testing measures live throughput by running the application
Static analysis requires executing the code with test data

questions.explanation: Static testing examines artifacts without execution and can reveal ambiguity. Dynamic testing observes behavior through execution; live throughput is dynamic and failure observations may need further diagnosis. Static analysis examines code without executing it. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.3 (p. 34); FL-3.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A review is author-led and takes participants through a work product to build understanding and gather findings. Which review type best fits?

options.text: Informal review
Walkthrough
Inspection
Technical review

questions.explanation: A walkthrough is led by the author and can serve objectives such as educating reviewers, building understanding and detecting anomalies. A technical review is led by a moderator, an inspection does not let the author lead, and an informal review follows no defined process. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.4 (p. 36); FL-3.2.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester derives cases from source-code control flow. What makes these white-box cases?

options.text: They are written by the original developer
They are necessarily automated
Their coverage items come from internal structure
They require a user representative to choose inputs

questions.explanation: The basis for derivation defines the technique family. Automation, author identity and stakeholder participation do not by themselves make a case white-box. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.1 (p. 39); FL-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A function runs both outcomes of each modeled conditional decision. What evidence is established?

options.text: Consistent behavior in future configurations
Full branch coverage
Completion of requirements-based acceptance
Execution of each input-data combination

questions.explanation: Executing both outcomes covers the corresponding branches. It does not exhaust input combinations, detect omitted functionality or guarantee behavior in other environments. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 (p. 43); FL-4.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: An implementation omits a required surcharge rule entirely, yet its existing code reaches 100% branch coverage. What is the limitation?

options.text: Reachable code can still omit required business rules
Full branch coverage includes absent requirements
The omission makes coverage calculations undefined
Branch coverage measures stakeholder satisfaction

questions.explanation: Coverage measures the structure that exists. A missing business rule needs requirements-based evidence; neither coverage alone nor stakeholder satisfaction can be inferred from code reachability. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.3 (p. 43); FL-4.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team organizes exploratory testing around 60-minute charters. What should it retain for useful accountability?

options.text: A claim of complete requirements coverage
A detailed test script written before the session
Observations, tested areas and a session debrief
A fixed sequence that forbids adapting to discoveries

questions.explanation: Session-based exploratory testing uses a charter and a time box, records steps and discoveries, for example on session sheets, and ends with a debriefing. One session cannot claim complete coverage, and fixed sequences or pre-written scripts contradict designing tests while learning. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 (p. 44); FL-4.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester uses a list of common accessibility and validation conditions, choosing detailed inputs during execution. Which technique fits?

options.text: A formal decision table
Checklist-based testing
A fully specified execution script
Branch coverage analysis

questions.explanation: The list guides what to check while leaving detailed cases to judgment. A script prescribes steps more tightly; branches and decision tables derive from different coverage models. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 (p. 44); FL-4.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO valid styles for documenting acceptance criteria.

options.text: Plan-oriented, such as exit criteria
Rule-oriented, such as a verification list
Defect-oriented, such as severity ratings
Code-oriented, such as branch conditions
Scenario-oriented, such as Given/When/Then

questions.explanation: The two most common formats for acceptance criteria are scenario-oriented, for example Given/When/Then, and rule-oriented, for example a bullet-point verification list or an input-output table. Branch conditions, severity ratings and exit criteria are not acceptance-criteria formats. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.2 (p. 45); FL-4.5.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: An input has four specified equivalence partitions. A suite exercises representatives of three different partitions. What is its equivalence-partition coverage?
questions.explanation: Coverage is exercised partitions divided by total partitions: 3/4 × 100 = 75%. The number of values within each exercised partition does not alter this measure; the fourth partition remains uncovered. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A temperature accepts integers 10–20 inclusive. Considering the valid partition boundary values 10 and 20, which set exercises each of these values and both of its immediate neighbors?
questions.explanation: For the specified valid-partition boundaries, exercise 9/10/11 and 19/20/21. Four points omit their inside neighbors; distant or exclusively valid points miss stated coverage items. This question targets boundary values 10 and 20; full three-value coverage across all partition boundaries would also include 8 and 22. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: Rule: a member receives a discount regardless of coupon; a non-member receives it only with a valid coupon. Which TWO combinations receive a discount?

options.text: Non-member with no valid coupon
Member with no coupon
Non-member with a valid coupon
Non-member with an invalid coupon
Non-member with an expired coupon

questions.explanation: Membership alone grants the discount; a valid coupon grants it to a non-member. Both non-member distractors lack a valid coupon, so the specified rule denies the discount. An expired coupon is not valid, so it gives a non-member no discount. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 (p. 41); FL-4.2.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: States are Draft, Submitted and Approved. Valid transitions are Draft→Submitted, Submitted→Draft and Submitted→Approved. Starting Draft, a test submits then approves. Which uncovered transition must another test exercise for full valid-transition coverage?

options.text: Return from Approved to Draft
Move from Draft directly to Approved
Move from Approved to Submitted
Return from Submitted to Draft

questions.explanation: Submit then approve covers two of the three listed transitions. The remaining valid transition is Submitted→Draft. The other transitions are not defined as valid in this model. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 (p. 41); FL-4.2.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: Criterion: after three consecutive failed logins, an account locks; a successful login before lock resets the count. Which sequence tests the reset behavior?

options.text: Fail, succeed, fail; account becomes locked
Fail, fail, succeed, fail; account remains unlocked
Succeed, fail, fail; account becomes locked
Fail, fail, fail; account remains unlocked

questions.explanation: The successful third attempt resets the count, so the final failure is the first of a new sequence. Three consecutive failures should lock; one or two failures after reset should not. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: Which distribution best reflects the test pyramid?

options.text: A ban on testing user workflows
Many small checks and fewer broad end-to-end checks
The same number of checks at every scope
Few component checks and many broad end-to-end checks

questions.explanation: The pyramid encourages a broad base of small, fast checks and a smaller set of broad checks. It does not demand identical counts or eliminate end-to-end evidence. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.6 (p. 50); FL-5.1.6 (K1).

questions.prompt: An environment must be ready before system execution begins; an agreed defect threshold must be met before it finishes. How are these criteria classified?

options.text: Both are exit because they refer to quality
Environment readiness is entry; defect threshold is exit
Environment readiness is exit; defect threshold is entry
Both are entry because they refer to testing

questions.explanation: Entry conditions enable starting an activity; exit conditions enable completion. Their function, rather than the words “environment” or “defect,” determines the classification. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.3 (p. 49); FL-5.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A load test critiques throughput using technical measures. Which testing quadrant best fits?

options.text: Q1: technology-facing support for development
Q4: technology-facing product evaluation
Q2: business-facing support for development
Q3: business-facing product evaluation

questions.explanation: Load and technical performance evaluation belong in Q4. Q1 concerns development-supporting technical checks; Q2 acceptance examples support work; Q3 assesses business-facing product use. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.7 (p. 51); FL-5.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: A payment failure has greater assessed product risk than a cosmetic issue. How should that influence testing?

options.text: Treat the risk ranking as proof of a future failure
Delete every test outside the payment area
Use the same effort regardless of risk differences
Investigate payment behavior more thoroughly

questions.explanation: Risk analysis guides effort, techniques and scope. It need not eliminate all lower-risk checks, ignore differences or predict with certainty that a failure will occur. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.3 (p. 52); FL-5.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A remote release team includes engineers and business managers. How should test status be communicated?

options.text: Use a private conversation instead of an accessible record
Send unexplained logs and expect similar interpretation
Summarize implications and link technical detail
Omit blocked cases until test execution has finished

questions.explanation: Different audiences need different detail; shared summaries and linked evidence support understanding. Unexplained logs, private-only discussion and hidden blockers undermine informed decisions. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.3 (p. 55); FL-5.3.3 (K2).
