questions.prompt: A rerun uses updated data with the same build and test procedure and now passes. What configuration information is essential to interpret the change?

options.text: The approval date of the test procedure
The priority recorded in the original defect report
The build identifier, which both runs share
The versions of the test data used in each run

questions.explanation: Only the data changed between the runs, so identifying both data versions explains the different outcome and keeps results reproducible. The shared build and procedure cannot explain the change, and defect priority or approval dates are not the configuration of the run. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.4 (p. 56); FL-5.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Historical testing effort is 25% of development effort for comparable work. Development is estimated at 160 hours. Using that ratio, what is the testing estimate?

options.text: 120 hours
64 hours
40 hours
25 hours

questions.explanation: The ratio gives 0.25 × 160 = 40 hours. Twenty-five treats a percentage as hours; sixty-four uses the wrong ratio; 120 is the remaining share rather than testing effort. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: Risk priorities are Payment highest, Search medium, Profile lowest. Payment requires Account Setup first. No other dependencies apply. Which ordering honors risk and dependencies?

options.text: Payment, Account Setup, Search, Profile
Account Setup, Payment, Search, Profile
Profile, Search, Account Setup, Payment
Search, Profile, Payment, Account Setup

questions.explanation: Setup must precede Payment even though Payment has the highest risk. Once the prerequisite is met, Payment comes before medium and low risk. The other orders violate dependency or unnecessarily defer the highest risk. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: A mobile crash occurs only for an offline session with a cached cart. Which defect-report precondition is most useful?

options.text: State that the crash happens on mobile devices
Reference the test charter used for the session
Identify build, device, network mode and stored cart data
Set the severity to critical and the priority to high

questions.explanation: The failure depends on specific conditions, so the report must identify the test object version, environment and data needed to reproduce it. A vague platform statement does not allow reproduction, and severity, priority and charter references are other report fields rather than reproduction preconditions. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tool flags unreachable code and coding-rule violations without executing the application. Which category fits?

options.text: Performance testing
Test execution
Service virtualization
Static analysis

questions.explanation: Static analysis inspects structured work products without running them. Performance and execution tools observe runtime behavior; virtualization supplies substitutes for dependencies rather than performs this analysis. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.1 (p. 59); FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which risk should be considered when adopting a record-and-playback interface tool?

options.text: The certainty that every recorded action detects a defect
The inability to automate any repeatable checks
The disappearance of all execution-time savings
Maintenance costs when screen layout and controls change

questions.explanation: Interface scripts can be fragile and require maintenance after changes. This is a risk to evaluate, not a claim that automation never saves time or that every action detects a defect. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.2 (p. 59); FL-6.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Select TWO typical test objectives.

options.text: Repair the defects found during test execution
Validate that the product meets stakeholder needs
Verify that specified requirements are fulfilled
Define the organization's development process
Prove that the product contains no defects

questions.explanation: Verifying fulfilment of specified requirements and validating that the test object works as stakeholders expect are typical objectives. Testing cannot prove the absence of defects, repairing defects is debugging, and defining development processes is a quality-assurance concern. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.1.1 (p. 15); FL-1.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which practice fits a whole-team approach to quality?

options.text: Every team member must perform the same daily tasks
Testers help colleagues develop useful testing skills
Business representatives avoid acceptance discussions
Developers delegate all quality concerns to a separate team

questions.explanation: Sharing expertise helps the team contribute to quality. Delegating all quality, excluding business input or requiring identical duties contradicts complementary contributions. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.2 (p. 22); FL-1.5.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: A programmer misreads a rule, writes a wrong comparison, and an eligible customer is rejected. What is the observed rejection?

options.text: An error
A failure
A root cause
A defect

questions.explanation: The rejection is observed incorrect behavior, a failure. Misreading is the human error; the comparison is the defect; an underlying reason for the mistake would be a root cause. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.3 (p. 17); FL-1.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Most discovered defects are concentrated in two modules. Which testing response uses the clustering principle sensibly?

options.text: Attribute the defects to module size without investigation
Focus investigation there and assess remaining risks
Infer that the remaining modules are defect-free
Remove regression checks from the affected modules

questions.explanation: Clustering guides focused investigation but does not prove unexamined areas safe. Removing regression or reducing every cause to size is unsupported by the observation. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.3 (p. 17); FL-1.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Cases have been designed. The tester now prepares accounts, data and an execution sequence. Which activity is the main focus?

options.text: Test monitoring
Test analysis
Test implementation
Test completion

questions.explanation: Implementation prepares runnable testware and environments. Analysis identifies conditions, monitoring tracks progress, and completion consolidates finished work. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.1 (p. 18); FL-1.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Requirement-to-test links show that a high-risk requirement has no associated case. What does this expose?

options.text: A guarantee that adding one case will eliminate its risk
Missing planned coverage for that high-risk behavior
Proof that existing test results are incorrect
Proof that the implementation is defective

questions.explanation: Traceability can reveal missing planned coverage. The gap is not proof of a code defect or incorrect earlier results, and one case cannot guarantee removal of every associated risk. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.4 (p. 20); FL-1.4.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which task most directly belongs to the test-management role?

options.text: Prepare the detailed data for one test case
Derive individual boundary-value inputs
Coordinate resources and monitor test progress
Execute a specified API check

questions.explanation: Coordination and monitoring are management responsibilities. Input derivation, execution and detailed data preparation are technical testing activities, although one person can perform both roles. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.5 (p. 21); FL-1.4.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester examines an unexpected result and designs a follow-up to distinguish two possible explanations. Which skill is most directly demonstrated?

options.text: Being a team player
Domain knowledge
Analytical thinking
Active listening

questions.explanation: Designing a test that discriminates between possible explanations applies analytical and critical thinking. Active listening and teamwork concern interaction with others, and domain knowledge concerns understanding the business; none is the focus here. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.1 (p. 21); FL-1.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why establish objectives and an appropriate basis for each test level?

options.text: To ensure all levels find identical defects
To avoid reviewing development artifacts
To require all tests to run on production data
To focus evaluation on the purpose of its stage

questions.explanation: Objectives and a basis focus checks and expected results at each level. Levels need not find the same defect types, and neither reviews nor controlled test data are excluded. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.2 (p. 25); FL-2.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which approach collaboratively derives acceptance tests before implementing a user story?

options.text: Acceptance test-driven development
Acceptance coverage measurement
Defect trend monitoring
Exploratory session management

questions.explanation: ATDD uses agreed acceptance examples to guide implementation. Exploratory management organizes investigations; statement analysis evaluates structure; defect trends support monitoring. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.3 (p. 26); FL-2.1.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: A payroll application exchanges files with an external bank service. Tests check that interaction. Which level is the primary focus?

options.text: System integration testing
User acceptance testing
Component integration testing
Component testing

questions.explanation: Interactions between systems or external services are the focus of system integration. Lower levels target components; user acceptance checks readiness for stakeholder needs rather than this interface specifically. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.1 (p. 28); FL-2.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A repaired defect is checked with the inputs that originally triggered it. What is the primary purpose?

options.text: Confirmation that the specific failure no longer occurs
Replacement of checks for adverse effects elsewhere
Discovery of the developer's original reasoning mistake
Measurement of every branch in the system

questions.explanation: Confirmation testing evaluates the repaired behavior. Debugging investigates causes; branch measurement is structural coverage; regression remains needed for possible side effects. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.3 (p. 30); FL-2.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A retrospective compares promised improvement actions with results from the next iteration. Why is this useful?

options.text: Assess whether the change was effective
It replaces collecting test execution evidence
It certifies future iterations as defect-free
It imposes identical practices across different teams

questions.explanation: Reviewing effects supports evidence-based process improvement. It cannot certify future iterations, replace product testing or prescribe one process for all contexts. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.6 (p. 28); FL-2.1.6 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO ways DevOps can support testing.

options.text: Continuous deployment proves every requirement is correct
Pipeline tools eliminate the need for test design
Cross-functional collaboration reduces handover friction
Automated checks provide faster delivery feedback
It removes the need for manual testing from a user's perspective

questions.explanation: DevOps practices can speed feedback and improve collaboration. Deployment itself does not prove correctness, and useful automated checks still require thoughtful design. Manual testing from the user's perspective is still needed in DevOps. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.4 (p. 26); FL-2.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which item is suitable for a review-based static test?

options.text: A timing benchmark that runs the application
A proposed test case with expected results
An executed user session on a new binary
A live throughput experiment on a running service

questions.explanation: A test case can be reviewed as a work product, including its expectations. Throughput experiments, executed sessions and timing benchmarks run software and are dynamic activities. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.1 (p. 33); FL-3.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which review role records findings and agreed decisions during a meeting?

options.text: Scribe
Author
Moderator
Review manager

questions.explanation: The scribe documents findings and decisions. The moderator facilitates, the author owns the artifact, and management provides organizational support rather than this recording duty. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.3 (p. 36); FL-3.2.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: A review detects a missing rule; a runtime test reveals an incorrect output. Which distinction is accurate?

options.text: Both activities require executing the application
Static checks expose defects; dynamic checks expose failures
The missing rule can be found only through runtime coverage
The incorrect output is the human mistake itself

questions.explanation: Static review can directly reveal an omission. Dynamic execution produces an observed failure. Neither requires static review to run software, and the output is not itself a human error. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.3 (p. 34); FL-3.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: The review meeting has classified anomalies and agreed changes. Which activity closes the loop?

options.text: Replacing the artifact with execution logs
Starting a new review without tracking the changes
Fixing the work product and reporting follow-up results
Discarding findings after the meeting ends

questions.explanation: Fixing and reporting ensure findings lead to changes and tracked outcomes. Discarding or losing links prevents closure; execution logs are not a substitute for the reviewed artifact. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.2 (p. 35); FL-3.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester selects malformed dates because previous projects often mishandled them. Which family of techniques is the main basis?

options.text: Control-flow coverage
White-box
Experience-based
Black-box decision-table analysis

questions.explanation: The selection is driven by past defect experience, so it is experience-based error guessing. No structural model or explicitly analyzed condition table is given. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.1 (p. 39); FL-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A program has an if statement without an else, followed by a statement that runs for every input. Tests take only the true path. Why can statement coverage be complete while branch coverage is incomplete?

options.text: Branch coverage excludes conditional decisions
Statement coverage counts requirements rather than code
All statements can run without taking the false outcome
The false outcome adds an executable else statement by definition

questions.explanation: The true path can execute both the conditional body and following statement. The false outcome is still unexecuted even without an else body. Statement coverage concerns code, and decisions contribute branches. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.1 (p. 42); FL-4.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO appropriate interpretations of full structural coverage.

options.text: It establishes exhaustive coverage of input combinations
It can coexist with incorrect expected behavior
It provides evidence that modeled code items were exercised
It certifies implementation of omitted business rules
It removes the need for black-box tests of the same code

questions.explanation: Structural reachability is valuable but independent of whether results are correct. Missing rules and all combinations require evidence beyond the covered structure. White-box coverage complements black-box testing rather than replacing it. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.3 (p. 43); FL-4.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester uses a fault checklist built from incidents: null input, duplicate submission and rounding errors. What is the main reason these cases were selected?

options.text: A complete table of all Boolean combinations
A requirement to execute every branch
A model of all states and transitions
Knowledge of plausible developer mistakes

questions.explanation: Incident-based fault ideas are error guessing. The stem does not describe branch coverage, a decision table or a state model as the derivation basis. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 (p. 43); FL-4.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why review and update a testing checklist after a new category of failures appears?

options.text: To keep its guidance relevant to current risks
To turn it into proof of exhaustive testing
To remove the need for observations during execution
To forbid testers from using judgment

questions.explanation: A checklist evolves with risks and experience. Updating it neither guarantees completeness nor removes judgment and recording of actual behavior. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 (p. 44); FL-4.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A user story states a requested feature but omits why the user needs it. What should the conversation clarify?

options.text: The exact database table names before discussing behavior
The tester's preferred automation framework
The total number of future regression scripts
The user's goal and the value of the capability

questions.explanation: Understanding user value helps judge desired behavior and examples. Implementation names, framework preferences and speculative script counts do not resolve the missing need. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 (p. 45); FL-4.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A form has three payment-method partitions and two delivery-method partitions. Every combination is feasible. What is the minimum number of cases to cover each partition of both inputs, without requiring combination coverage?
questions.explanation: Three cases can cover the three payment partitions and include both delivery partitions, for example P1/D1, P2/D2 and P3/D1. Two cannot cover three payment partitions; six covers all combinations, a stronger requirement than stated. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A balance rule accepts amounts 100.00–200.00 inclusive, with resolution 0.01. Which pair checks the lower boundary using two-value BVA?
questions.explanation: The boundary is 100.00 and the closest point across it is 99.99 at the stated resolution. Interior neighbors apply to three-value analysis; one-unit jumps are not immediate neighbors. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: Access requires authentication and either admin status or an active subscription. Which TWO cases are permitted?

options.text: Unauthenticated admin with active subscription
Authenticated non-admin without subscription
Authenticated non-admin with active subscription
Authenticated admin without subscription
Unauthenticated non-admin with active subscription

questions.explanation: Authentication is mandatory. After it, either admin status or active subscription suffices. One distractor lacks authentication; the other satisfies neither of the alternative granting conditions. Without authentication, an active subscription does not grant access. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 (p. 41); FL-4.2.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: A session model has transitions Anonymous→SignedIn on login, SignedIn→Anonymous on logout and SignedIn→Expired on timeout. Tests login and logout only. What is state coverage?
questions.explanation: Anonymous and SignedIn are visited, but Expired is not. The denominator is the three modeled states, not the executed events; transition coverage is a different metric even where values coincide. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 (p. 41); FL-4.2.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: Acceptance rules say cancellations before shipment return the full payment; cancellations after shipment are refused. Which example exposes an implementation that incorrectly refunds shipped orders?

options.text: Given Shipped, cancel; expect refusal and no refund
Given Shipped, cancel; expect a full refund
Given Unshipped, cancel; expect refusal
Given Unshipped, cancel; expect a full refund

questions.explanation: The correct case applies the negative rule to a shipped order. The valid unshipped case does not expose this defect; the other choices encode expectations contrary to the agreed rules. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: Which two factors express the level of a risk?

options.text: Test coverage and risk impact
Risk likelihood and risk impact
Risk likelihood and test effort
Defect severity and fix priority

questions.explanation: A risk is characterized by its likelihood (the probability of occurrence) and its impact (the consequences); together they express the risk level. Test effort and coverage are responses to risk, and severity and priority classify defects rather than risks. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.1 (p. 52); FL-5.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A plan states the test approach but omits people and environments needed. What is the practical consequence?

options.text: Resource feasibility and responsibilities remain unclear
Every planned test automatically becomes invalid
The approach no longer describes any testing activity
The test results become available without execution

questions.explanation: Plans need resources and responsibilities to support delivery. Missing them creates uncertainty but does not automatically invalidate all cases or manufacture execution evidence. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.1 (p. 48); FL-5.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Automated component checks support developers while code is being built. Which quadrant fits their primary role?

options.text: Q3: business-facing critique
Q4: technology-facing critique
Q1: technology-facing support
Q2: business-facing support

questions.explanation: Component checks supporting development belong in Q1. Q2 uses business-facing guidance, while Q3 and Q4 primarily critique the product from their respective perspectives. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.7 (p. 51); FL-5.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: A high-impact data-loss risk is identified. Which TWO responses can help address it?

options.text: Increase recovery testing and verify mitigation controls
Hide blocked recovery checks from the release report
Explicitly document residual risk for an informed acceptance decision
Assume the risk disappears after its first passing test
Lower the risk's impact rating so it falls below the threshold

questions.explanation: Mitigation evidence and informed residual-risk acceptance are valid responses. One passing check cannot erase the risk, and concealing missing evidence prevents sound decisions. Re-rating a risk without new evidence does not reduce it. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.4 (p. 53); FL-5.2.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: How does a test completion report primarily differ from a progress report?

options.text: It replaces detailed defect records with personal judgments
It consolidates milestone outcomes and remaining risk
It is only a list of future execution steps
It must contain no testing results

questions.explanation: Completion reporting consolidates achieved results, deviations and remaining risk. It can reference detailed findings but is not a future procedure or an appraisal of people. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.2 (p. 54); FL-5.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A release baseline is used for testing. What should it identify?

options.text: The defects that must be fixed before release
A promise that no later changes will occur
The agreed versions of related product and test items
An unordered collection of whatever files are newest

questions.explanation: A baseline records approved versions of configuration items, which can then change only through formal change control and can be restored to reproduce results. It does not forbid change, is not simply the newest files, and is not a list of defects to fix. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.4 (p. 56); FL-5.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team estimates 30 comparable cases remaining. Its observed execution rate is 6 cases per hour, with setup already complete. What is the extrapolated execution effort?

options.text: 24 hours
6 hours
5 hours
180 hours

questions.explanation: Effort is remaining cases divided by rate: 30/6=5 hours. Six repeats the rate, 24 subtracts quantities with different units, and 180 multiplies where division is needed. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: Requirement priorities are R1 highest, R2 medium, R3 lowest. T1 checks R3, T2 checks R1 and T3 checks R2. There are no dependencies. Using requirements-based prioritization, what is the order?
questions.explanation: Order cases by their requirements’ priorities: the case for R1 is T2, then R2 is T3, then R3 is T1. Case numbers do not determine priority, and the absence of dependencies means the stated priority order can be applied directly. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: A reproducible issue loses customer data but the report calls it “cosmetic.” Which report field should be corrected to reflect observed consequences?

options.text: Reporter name
Submission timestamp
Severity
Test-case identifier

questions.explanation: Severity describes impact, so data loss is inconsistent with a cosmetic classification. Identity, reference and time fields do not communicate the seriousness of the failure. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team needs to organize cases, execution status and requirement coverage in one place. Which tool category is the best fit?

options.text: Test design and implementation
Static testing
Collaboration
Test management

questions.explanation: Test management tools manage requirements, tests, defects and configuration to make the test process more efficient. Static testing tools support reviews and static analysis, test design tools generate cases and data, and collaboration tools facilitate communication. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.1 (p. 59); FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO risks of test automation.

options.text: Consistent execution in the same order and frequency
Relying on the tool instead of critical thinking
Unrealistic expectations about the tool's benefits
More time for testers to design deeper tests
Less manual effort for repetitive regression runs

questions.explanation: Unrealistic expectations about a tool's benefits and over-reliance on the tool at the expense of human critical thinking are listed risks. Reduced repetitive work, consistent execution and more time for designing tests are potential benefits. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.2 (p. 59); FL-6.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which activity is primarily quality assurance rather than product testing?

options.text: Measuring service response time under load
Reviewing a particular user story for contradictions
Improving the review process to prevent recurring omissions
Executing a checkout case and comparing the total

questions.explanation: Process improvement is QA-oriented prevention. Executing, measuring and reviewing specific work products are product evaluation activities, including static and dynamic testing. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.2 (p. 17); FL-1.2.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which behavior best supports shared quality responsibility?

options.text: Business representatives avoid clarifying examples
Collaborate on investigating failures and improving checks
Developers stop running checks once a tester joins
Testers conceal findings until the end of an iteration

questions.explanation: Joint investigation and improvement combine skills and support ownership. Abandoning checks, concealing evidence and avoiding clarification reduce the team's ability to address quality. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.2 (p. 22); FL-1.5.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: A team finds that repeated requirement mistakes stem from excluding domain experts from refinement. What does that exclusion represent in this investigation?

options.text: A root cause
A runtime failure
The expected output of a test
An executable defect

questions.explanation: The exclusion is an underlying reason for recurring mistakes. It is not an observed runtime failure, code flaw or expected result; addressing it can help prevent repetition. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.3 (p. 17); FL-1.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A unchanged suite keeps passing, while recent incidents expose risks it never checked. Which response addresses tests wearing out?

options.text: Treat repeat passes as proof that incidents are unrelated
Refresh cases using evolving conditions
Rename existing passing cases without changing coverage
Remove the suite and stop regression testing

questions.explanation: Refreshing cases can reveal problems missed by unchanged checks. Renaming does not change evidence; passing old checks does not dismiss incidents, and useful regression still has value. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.3 (p. 17); FL-1.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A lead compares executed tests with the plan, then moves engineers to unblock high-risk cases. Which TWO activities are represented?

options.text: Test design
Test control
Test completion
Test monitoring
Test analysis

questions.explanation: Comparing actual progress with plans is monitoring; changing actions in response is control. The scenario does not derive new cases or consolidate a completed milestone. No test conditions are being identified, so test analysis is not represented. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.1 (p. 18); FL-1.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A project has a strict regulatory evidence requirement. How should that context affect its test process?

options.text: Remove documentation because execution is sufficient
Plan suitable traceability, records and review responsibilities
Treat tool selection as the sole compliance activity
Use the process from an unrelated informal prototype unchanged

questions.explanation: Context shapes evidence and responsibilities as well as execution. Copying an unsuitable approach, relying solely on tools or discarding records does not address the stated constraint. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.2 (p. 19); FL-1.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A defect is linked to its failing case, execution and original requirement. Which TWO uses do these links support?

options.text: Guaranteeing all other requirements pass
Automatically proving the root cause
Assessing which requirement is affected
Understanding the evidence behind the finding
Replacing the need for a defect report

questions.explanation: Links support impact and evidence assessment. They cannot by themselves diagnose causes or establish results for unrelated requirements. Traceability supplements defect reports rather than replacing them. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.4 (p. 20); FL-1.4.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: A separate testing group finds defects but has little contact with developers and becomes a release bottleneck. What is the main drawback illustrated?

options.text: Developer checks are incompatible with independent testing
All testing must therefore be performed by authors
Organizational isolation can delay delivery
Independent perspectives cannot reveal new defects

questions.explanation: The issue is isolation and bottlenecking, a possible drawback of independence. Independent perspective can still be useful, and it can coexist with developer checks without forcing one universal staffing model. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.3 (p. 22); FL-1.5.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which good practice helps prevent downstream defects during development?

options.text: Wait for release packaging before considering testability
Assign every level an identical test basis
Involve testers in reviews of requirements and designs
Use production incidents as the first quality feedback

questions.explanation: Early tester involvement can expose ambiguity and testability problems. Waiting for packaging or incidents loses early feedback; test bases and objectives differ by level. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.2 (p. 25); FL-2.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which sequence best describes the core TDD cycle?

options.text: Write a failing test, make it pass, then refactor
Write acceptance criteria, then a test plan, then code
Refactor, then write the code, then write tests
Write the code, then write tests, then refactor

questions.explanation: TDD directs coding through tests: a test is written first, code is written to satisfy it, and then tests and code are refactored. Writing code before tests reverses the approach, and the other sequences do not describe the TDD cycle. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.3 (p. 26); FL-2.1.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: Tests are derived from source branches and assert the computed results. Which description is accurate?

options.text: They cannot check behavior because structure was used
They use white-box derivation and can still check functional behavior
They belong to acceptance level solely because assertions exist
They are static because the source was consulted

questions.explanation: A structural basis makes derivation white-box, but execution and assertions can assess behavior. Source knowledge does not make execution static or determine the test level. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.2 (p. 29); FL-2.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: An old service is being retired, with data retained for future audit. What maintenance-testing concern is appropriate?

options.text: Verify the archival and retrieval arrangements
Rerun an unrelated interface test without impact analysis
Test only features added to the retired service next year
Assume retirement makes retained data irrelevant

questions.explanation: Retirement can require verification of archival access and retention. Future features, ignoring data or choosing unrelated checks do not address the stated operational change. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.3 (p. 31); FL-2.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A sequential project maps planned acceptance testing to stakeholder needs and system testing to system requirements. What benefit does that mapping provide?

options.text: Proof that execution can find every possible defect
An obligation to use identical cases at all levels
A requirement for testing to avoid early reviews
A suitable test basis and objectives at each level

questions.explanation: Mapping levels to corresponding work products supports focused planning and evaluation. It does not promise exhaustiveness, prohibit reviews or make different levels interchangeable. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.1 (p. 25); FL-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO statements consistent with shift left.

options.text: Review requirements before defects propagate into code
Eliminate all system testing once component tests exist
Move every acceptance decision before stakeholder examples are agreed
Design relevant checks earlier while retaining later evaluation
Postpone non-functional testing until a complete system exists

questions.explanation: Earlier suitable activities provide feedback sooner, while later evaluation remains important. Shift left neither eliminates system testing nor bypasses agreement on stakeholder expectations. Postponing non-functional testing is the opposite of shift left, which starts it at component level where possible. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.5 (p. 27); FL-2.1.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: Frequent feedback on small increments most directly helps a team do what?

options.text: Replace confirmation testing after defect fixes
Adjust understanding when stakeholder needs change
Guarantee that the original requirements never evolve
Avoid communicating about completed behavior

questions.explanation: Frequent feedback helps detect changed or misunderstood needs. It does not freeze requirements, remove communication or provide confirmation of a code fix by itself. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.1 (p. 35); FL-3.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which review practice supports a constructive culture?

options.text: Reward reviewers for agreeing regardless of evidence
Use findings to rank individual authors publicly
Discuss defects in the work product using clear evidence
Prevent clarification questions to shorten the meeting

questions.explanation: Focusing on work-product evidence supports useful evaluation. Public ranking, pressured agreement and suppressed clarification undermine review goals and psychological safety. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.5 (p. 37); FL-3.2.5 (K1).

questions.prompt: A static analysis tool flags unreachable code before execution. What benefit can this provide?

options.text: Measured evidence of peak-load response time
Early detection of flaws in source structure
A guarantee that every flagged issue is a user-visible failure
Replacement of requirements-based testing

questions.explanation: Static analysis can detect structural issues before dynamic testing. It does not measure runtime load, guarantee user-visible consequences for every finding or replace requirements evidence. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.2 (p. 33); FL-3.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team chooses the most formal review type, with defined roles, prescribed steps and collected review information. Which type best fits?

options.text: Author-led walkthrough
Inspection
Informal review
Exploratory session

questions.explanation: Inspection is the most formal review type. Informal reviews have fewer prescribed steps, walkthroughs are typically author-led, and exploratory sessions execute and investigate software rather than review an artifact this way. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.4 (p. 36); FL-3.2.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why combine specification-based and structure-based techniques?

options.text: They ensure each technique finds identical defects
They make experience-based investigation unusable
They expose different coverage gaps
They remove the need for expected outcomes

questions.explanation: Requirements coverage and structural reachability address different omissions. Combining them broadens evidence without guaranteeing identical findings, removing oracles or excluding experience-based work. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.1 (p. 39); FL-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A suite reports 80% statement coverage. Which interpretation is justified?

options.text: Exactly 20% of decision outcomes were not taken
Exactly 20% of the product's defects remain
Some executable statements were not exercised
Exactly 20% of requirements are missing

questions.explanation: Statement coverage describes executed statements. It cannot be converted directly into requirements, branches or defect percentages; those need their own evidence. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.1 (p. 42); FL-4.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO accurate statements about branch coverage.

options.text: Full statement coverage necessarily includes full branch coverage
It measures exercised control-flow branches
Full branch coverage includes full statement coverage for the modeled structure
It measures the percentage of requirements accepted by users
Unconditional branches are excluded from branch coverage

questions.explanation: Branches concern control-flow choices, and covering all modeled branches also reaches their statements. The reverse implication fails; requirements acceptance is a different measure. Branch coverage counts both conditional and unconditional branches. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 (p. 43); FL-4.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester anticipates an off-by-one error after studying a team's recurring mistakes and adds a targeted case. What is the main technique?

options.text: Error-based execution scheduling
Formal review inspection
Error guessing
Configuration baselining

questions.explanation: A plausible fault based on experience motivates error guessing. Scheduling and baselining organize work and versions; inspection reviews a work product rather than derives this runtime case. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 (p. 43); FL-4.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: During exploratory testing, an unexpected save behavior is observed. What is an appropriate next step?

options.text: Declare complete coverage from the first session
Design a focused experiment and record what it reveals
Stop the session and wait for a written specification
Ignore it because it was absent from the initial charter

questions.explanation: In exploratory testing, design and execution evolve as the tester learns, so an unexpected result should guide a focused follow-up whose outcome is recorded. Coverage cannot be declared from one session, waiting for a specification abandons the approach, and a charter guides rather than restricts investigation. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 (p. 44); FL-4.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Criterion: “The screen should feel nice.” What is its main weakness as acceptance criteria?

options.text: It requires a specific implementation algorithm
It specifies a test framework too precisely
It contains too many measurable thresholds
It lacks an agreed observable basis for evaluation

questions.explanation: The phrase gives no shared observable expectation. The problem is ambiguity, rather than excessive detail or prescribed tools and implementation. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.2 (p. 45); FL-4.5.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A shipping result has four output partitions: domestic free, domestic paid, international paid and rejected address. Existing cases produce both domestic outputs and a rejected address. Which additional case closes the output-partition gap?

options.text: An international address producing rejection
An international address producing paid delivery
A domestic address producing free delivery
A domestic address producing paid delivery

questions.explanation: The suite has exercised three of the four specified output classes. An international paid-delivery outcome covers the remaining class. More examples of the already covered outputs do not close this partition gap. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: Integer scores have partitions below 50, 50–79 and 80 or above. Which set covers two-value BVA at both boundaries?
questions.explanation: The adjacent cross-partition pairs are 49/50 and 79/80. Other sets skip a boundary or the closest value across it, so they do not provide the requested boundary coverage. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A fee table has two Boolean conditions, Premium and Express. Premium=false with Express=true is infeasible. How many feasible rules remain in the full decision table?
questions.explanation: Two Boolean conditions initially give four combinations. Excluding the one stated infeasible combination leaves three. Two counts too few, four fails to exclude it, and eight introduces another condition. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 (p. 41); FL-4.2.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: From Ready, send moves to Waiting; from Waiting, reply moves to Done. Cancel is invalid in Waiting and must leave the state unchanged. Which test correctly checks the invalid transition?

options.text: Send, then cancel; expect state Done
Start Ready, then cancel; expect state Waiting
Send, then cancel; expect rejection and state Waiting
Send, then inspect; expect the initial state Ready

questions.explanation: Cancel from Waiting is explicitly invalid, so rejection with unchanged state is the correct expectation. The other tests cover valid behavior or states without attempting an invalid event. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 (p. 41); FL-4.2.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: Criterion: only active members can reserve; an active member cannot have more than two concurrent reservations. Which case tests the count restriction independently of membership eligibility?

options.text: Active member with no reservations adds one; expect refusal
Inactive member with two reservations adds one; expect success
Active member with two reservations adds one; expect refusal
Inactive member with no reservations adds one; expect refusal

questions.explanation: An eligible active member already at the limit isolates the count restriction. Inactive cases involve membership, and refusing the eligible empty account or accepting an inactive one contradicts the rules. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a test progress metric?

options.text: Mean time to failure of the system
Defect detection percentage
Number of test cases run and not run
Residual risk level of the release

questions.explanation: Test progress metrics include test cases run and not run, passed and failed, and implementation progress. Mean time to failure is a product quality metric, defect detection percentage is a defect metric and residual risk level is a risk metric. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.1 (p. 54); FL-5.3.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A completion criterion is unmet, but stakeholders consider releasing anyway. What is an appropriate response?

options.text: Delete evidence of the incomplete testing
Claim testing achieved its original objective unchanged
Report the deviation and residual risk for an explicit decision
Redefine the criterion silently to match current results

questions.explanation: Criteria support decisions rather than conceal uncertainty. Explicitly reporting deviations and risks permits an informed exception; silent changes and erased evidence misrepresent outcomes. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.3 (p. 49); FL-5.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: An agreed business-facing acceptance example guides implementation of a discount. Which quadrant best fits?

options.text: Q4: technology-facing product critique
Q1: technology-facing support for development
Q3: business-facing product critique
Q2: business-facing support for development

questions.explanation: The example guides work using business expectations, the purpose of Q2. Q1 concerns technical support, and Q3/Q4 primarily evaluate the finished product from different perspectives. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.7 (p. 51); FL-5.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: A supplier cannot deliver the test environment on schedule, while the product may leak confidential data. How are these risks classified?

options.text: Both are project because a deadline exists
Both are product because testing is involved
Environment delay is project; data leakage is product
Environment delay is product; data leakage is project

questions.explanation: The delay threatens project delivery; leakage threatens product quality. Context does not collapse these different consequences into one category. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.2 (p. 52); FL-5.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A dashboard shows 95% of executed tests passed but omits blocked security tests. What should a status update add?

options.text: A claim that the displayed pass percentage establishes readiness
The same percentage with more decimal places
The coverage gap and its implications for release risk
Names of people assigned to the blocked cases

questions.explanation: The missing high-risk evidence changes interpretation of the pass percentage. Precision or ownership alone is insufficient; the gap and decision implications must be communicated. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.3 (p. 55); FL-5.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Two runs of the same build and test procedure give different results. Select TWO items whose recorded versions are most relevant for explaining the difference.

options.text: The test data set used in each run
The risk register for the project
The template used for defect reports
The previous release's test completion report
The test environment configuration

questions.explanation: With the build and procedure unchanged, differences in test data or in the test environment can explain different results, so their versions must be identified. Completion reports, templates and the risk register are configuration items, but they do not determine the outcome of an individual run. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.4 (p. 56); FL-5.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: For a three-point estimate, use standard deviation SD=(P−O)/6. Optimistic effort is 6 days and pessimistic effort is 18 days. What is SD?

options.text: 3 days
2 days
6 days
12 days

questions.explanation: Substitute the bounds into the specified uncertainty formula: (18−6)/6=12/6=2 days. Twelve is the range before division; six is the optimistic input; neither is the standard deviation. This measure describes estimation uncertainty, not the expected effort. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: T1 covers A,B; T2 covers A,B,C,D; T3 covers E,F,G. No dependencies apply. Use coverage-based prioritization by total items covered, without recalculating additional coverage. What is the order?
questions.explanation: Total coverage counts are four for T2, three for T3 and two for T1. Descending totals give T2,T3,T1. The question explicitly asks for total coverage, so overlapping items are not removed after selecting a test. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: A reproducible data-loss issue has severe impact, but a documented workaround permits the release owner to schedule its fix later. Which report classification reflects impact separately from agreed urgency?

options.text: Low severity because the fix is scheduled later
Omit impact because a workaround has been approved
High severity with lower fix priority
High urgency solely because the title sounds serious

questions.explanation: Severity records the serious consequence of data loss; priority records the agreed urgency of remediation. A workaround can affect scheduling without making the underlying impact low. A title cannot establish urgency, and impact should remain documented. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: An unavailable payment gateway blocks tests. A tool supplies configurable responses in its place. What support is being used?

options.text: Defect trend reporting
Static analysis
Statement coverage measurement
Service virtualization

questions.explanation: Virtualization substitutes controlled behavior for a dependency. Static analysis inspects artifacts, coverage measures executed structure, and trends summarize findings rather than simulate the gateway. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.1 (p. 59); FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which is a potential risk of test automation?

options.text: Fewer human errors through repeatable execution
Earlier defect detection through faster execution
Depending on a vendor that may retire the tool
More objective measurement of achieved coverage

questions.explanation: Dependency on a tool vendor that may go out of business, retire or sell the tool is a listed risk of test automation. Objective coverage measurement, faster feedback and greater consistency are potential benefits. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.2 (p. 59); FL-6.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which purpose is a typical reason for evaluating software work products?

options.text: Proving the product is defect-free
Supporting a release decision
Removing the defects that cause failures
Improving the team's development process

questions.explanation: Testing supplies quality and risk information for stakeholder decisions such as release. Removing defects is debugging, improving processes is quality assurance, and testing cannot prove that a product is defect-free. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.1.1 (p. 15); FL-1.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: An engineer locates a memory leak and changes allocation logic. Which activity does this describe?

options.text: Debugging the implementation
Designing test conditions
Monitoring the schedule
Reviewing acceptance criteria

questions.explanation: Locating and repairing a cause is debugging. Case design, progress tracking and criteria review do not perform the repair described. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.1.2 (p. 16); FL-1.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A review exposes conflicting billing rules before implementation begins. How does this help?

options.text: It reduces avoidable rework later
It measures how fast billing runs are processed
It proves that the billing code will be correct
It removes the need to test billing after coding

questions.explanation: Finding the conflict before coding is a cost-effective way to detect a defect, so it is removed before it propagates into code and causes rework. A review cannot prove the later code correct, does not replace dynamic testing and does not measure performance. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.1 (p. 16); FL-1.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: What is the relationship between testing and quality assurance?

options.text: QA is performed only by the members of the test team
Testing improves processes; QA evaluates products
Testing evaluates products; QA improves processes
Testing and QA are two names for one activity

questions.explanation: Testing is product-oriented quality control, whereas QA is process-oriented, preventive and the responsibility of everyone on a project. The reversed pairing confuses the two, they are not the same activity, and QA is not limited to testers. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.2 (p. 17); FL-1.2.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Missing training leads an analyst to misunderstand a rule, write a faulty requirement, and cause incorrect charges when implemented. What is the faulty requirement?

options.text: A root cause in staff training
A defect in a work product
A failure observed by a user
An error made by the analyst

questions.explanation: The incorrect requirement is a defect. Misunderstanding is the error; missing training is a candidate root cause; observed wrong charges are failures. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.3 (p. 17); FL-1.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team adds new cases for newly introduced offline operation while retaining useful regression checks. Which principle explains this need?

options.text: Defects cluster in historically faulty areas
Exhaustive testing has a fixed duration
Context fixes the same number of cases
Tests lose effectiveness as risks evolve

questions.explanation: Repeated checks need review as new behavior and risks emerge. Clustering concerns concentrations of defects; the other options misstate exhaustiveness and context. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.3 (p. 17); FL-1.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester prepares scripts, orders procedures and configures data for an upcoming run. Which activity is described?

options.text: Test completion
Test implementation
Test analysis
Test monitoring

questions.explanation: Implementation prepares procedures, suites, data and environments. Analysis identifies what to test; monitoring assesses progress; completion consolidates milestone evidence. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.1 (p. 18); FL-1.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A prototype and a safety-critical controller have different consequences of failure. How should this affect their evaluation?

options.text: Prioritize the one with fewer end users
Adapt scope to their respective risks
Set equal effort using their line counts
Apply the same cases to both products

questions.explanation: Context, including consequences and risk, influences the approach. Line counts, shared code use and user counts alone cannot establish suitable scope or rigor. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.2 (p. 19); FL-1.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which work product results from turning conditions into detailed checks?

options.text: Logs with observed outcomes
Reports with residual risks
Directives with revised schedules
Cases with expected outcomes

questions.explanation: Design develops cases, inputs and expected results. Logs are execution outputs; residual-risk reports consolidate results; schedule directives are control outputs. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.3 (p. 20); FL-1.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A business rule changes and linked cases are identified immediately. What benefit is illustrated?

options.text: Environment provisioning
Impact assessment
Runtime load measurement
Automatic defect repair

questions.explanation: Traceability identifies affected testware when the basis changes. It does not itself measure load, repair the implementation or provision an environment. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.4 (p. 20); FL-1.4.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: One person coordinates staffing and another derives cases from requirements. Which pair of responsibilities fits?

options.text: Management role and testing role
Testing role and management role
Scribe role and reviewer role
Author role and moderator role

questions.explanation: Coordinating resources belongs to the test management role; deriving test cases is part of the testing role, which focuses on analysis, design, implementation and execution. The reversed pairing swaps them, and scribe, reviewer, author and moderator are review roles. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.5 (p. 21); FL-1.4.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: A report gives reproducible steps and separates observations from blame. Which skill is demonstrated?

options.text: Technical tool knowledge
Constructive communication
Domain knowledge
Curiosity and creativity

questions.explanation: Communicating defects factually and without blame is part of good communication skills, which matter because testers often bring bad news. Domain knowledge, tool knowledge and curiosity are other skills that the described report does not demonstrate. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.1 (p. 21); FL-1.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: In the whole-team approach, which responsibility is shared?

options.text: Approval of the release budget
Quality of the delivered product
Selection of the test management tool
Leadership of formal review meetings

questions.explanation: In the whole-team approach everyone shares responsibility for quality and brings complementary skills. Leading reviews, selecting tools and approving budgets are specific tasks, not responsibilities that the approach makes collective. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.2 (p. 22); FL-1.5.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: A separate group finds assumptions developers missed but struggles to obtain domain clarification. What does this illustrate?

options.text: Identical biases with reduced reporting effort
Shared implementation with easier data access
Different perspectives with a collaboration cost
Lower independence with faster diagnosis

questions.explanation: Independent perspectives can expose assumptions, while separation can impede communication. The other descriptions contradict the stated separation and clarification difficulty. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.3 (p. 22); FL-1.5.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team replaces a single large delivery with usable increments each fortnight. Which adjustment is appropriate?

options.text: Keep the original large-delivery schedule without revision
Check new and affected existing behavior in each increment
Defer product evaluation until the final increment arrives
Replace requirement review with one deployment approval

questions.explanation: Frequent increments need fast feedback and regression evidence alongside new-feature checks. Deferring evaluation or keeping an unadapted schedule misses the changed lifecycle. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.1 (p. 25); FL-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which practice applies across development lifecycles?

options.text: Replace planning with a final status report
Review drafts as they become available
Start case design after deployment
Give each level the same objective

questions.explanation: Early review of available work products is a lifecycle-independent good practice. Late design, identical objectives and replacing planning weaken evaluation. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.2 (p. 25); FL-2.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which sequence characterizes test-driven development?

options.text: Refactor existing code, then write tests for it
Implement a feature, deploy it, then draft its tests
Write a test, implement enough code, then refactor
Agree acceptance criteria, then code, then test

questions.explanation: Test-driven development writes the test first, then just enough code to pass it, and then refactors tests and code. The other sequences write code before its tests or describe acceptance-level work. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.3 (p. 26); FL-2.1.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: An organization integrates development and operations around frequent delivery. Which cost belongs in its plan?

options.text: Maintaining the pipeline and its checks
Removing representative data preparation
Replacing exploration with deployment logs
Avoiding integration between toolchains

questions.explanation: DevOps requires maintained delivery tools and automation resources. Data, human exploration and tool integration still require effort despite automated feedback. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.4 (p. 26); FL-2.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which action most clearly moves evaluation earlier?

options.text: Updating a completion report at retirement
Reviewing a draft interface contract
Repeating a case after a production fix
Archiving results after release approval

questions.explanation: Draft review can reveal defects before implementation. The other actions occur after production repair, release or retirement. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.5 (p. 27); FL-2.1.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team agrees to improve fixture provisioning in its retrospective. What completes the improvement loop?

options.text: Defer ownership until another incident
Rank team members by their suggestions
Replace the next backlog with meeting minutes
Check the effect in subsequent iterations

questions.explanation: Retrospectives support continuous improvement only when agreed improvements are followed up, so the team checks their effect in later iterations. Minutes do not replace the backlog, ranking people is not an objective, and deferring ownership leaves the action unimplemented. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.6 (p. 28); FL-2.1.6 (K2).

questions.prompt: A check exercises message exchange between a shop and an external bank. Which level describes this scope?

options.text: Component isolation testing
Component integration testing
Business acceptance testing
System integration testing

questions.explanation: Interfaces with external systems are system integration concerns. Internal units and their interactions have smaller scope; acceptance has stakeholder-readiness objectives. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.1 (p. 28); FL-2.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A check measures how quickly a report is produced under concurrent use. Which type describes its focus?

options.text: Confirmation testing
Functional rule testing
Static document review
Non-functional testing

questions.explanation: Response time under load is non-functional. There is no repaired defect or review described; the focus is performance rather than calculation rules. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.2 (p. 29); FL-2.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: After an address fix, the team repeats the original failure case and checks related delivery calculations. What are the respective purposes?

options.text: Static analysis and inspection
Monitoring and completion
Confirmation and regression
Acceptance and maintenance

questions.explanation: Repeating the failing case checks the repair; related calculations check adverse effects. The alternatives are other activities or contexts rather than these purposes. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.3 (p. 30); FL-2.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: An operational service moves to another storage provider. Which approach is appropriate?

options.text: Adopt old-provider results as the new baseline
Assess affected access, data and interfaces
Limit scope to edited application lines
Treat unchanged source as sufficient evidence

questions.explanation: Migration can alter data, interfaces and runtime behavior without source changes. Impact analysis guides maintenance scope; old results concern the previous configuration. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.3 (p. 31); FL-2.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which work product can be reviewed before executable software exists?

options.text: A draft API contract
A measured peak throughput
A recorded runtime heap size
A live request completion time

questions.explanation: A contract can be inspected for omissions and contradictions. Throughput, heap use and completion time are runtime observations requiring execution. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.1 (p. 33); FL-3.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A review finds conflicting eligibility rules. What is a direct benefit of resolving the finding?

options.text: Estimating observed transaction latency
Preventing downstream implementation defects
Measuring production resource consumption
Increasing executed branch coverage

questions.explanation: Early static findings can prevent propagation and rework. Review does not measure runtime consumption, reached branches or observed latency. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.2 (p. 33); FL-3.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which pairing lists a finding that a review can detect, followed by one that only execution reveals?

options.text: A timeout, then a contradiction
A contradiction, then a timeout
A slow response, then a memory leak
An ambiguity, then a naming violation

questions.explanation: A contradiction in a work product can be found directly by review, whereas a timeout is a failure observed only when the software runs. The reversed pair swaps the two, the slow response and leak are both runtime observations, and the ambiguity and naming violation are both static findings. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.3 (p. 34); FL-3.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: What benefit comes from early, frequent stakeholder feedback on drafts?

options.text: Freezing the requirements for the whole project
Removing the need for acceptance testing
Making regression testing unnecessary
Detecting misunderstood needs sooner

questions.explanation: Early and frequent feedback communicates potential quality problems early and prevents misunderstandings about requirements. It does not freeze requirements, since changes are expected, and it does not replace acceptance or regression testing. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.1 (p. 35); FL-3.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Participants examine a document separately and record candidate anomalies ahead of the discussion. Which activity is described?

options.text: Review initiation
Fixing and reporting
Communication and analysis
Individual review

questions.explanation: Individual review produces candidate findings. Initiation prepares participation; communication analyzes findings together; fixing and reporting follow agreed actions. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.2 (p. 35); FL-3.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Who records agreed findings during a formal review?

options.text: The author
The manager
The moderator
The scribe

questions.explanation: The scribe records findings and decisions. The author updates the work, management supports resources and the moderator facilitates discussion. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.3 (p. 36); FL-3.2.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: A review uses defined roles, preparation and metrics for process improvement. Which type is the most formal?

options.text: Inspection
Walkthrough
Informal review
Exploratory session

questions.explanation: Inspection is the most formal review type. Walkthroughs are generally author-led; informal reviews have less prescribed structure; exploration is a dynamic technique. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.4 (p. 36); FL-3.2.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which arrangement supports a useful review?

options.text: Manageable scope with preparation time
Large scope with immediate discussion
Public rankings of individual authors
Undocumented findings with rapid approval

questions.explanation: Manageable work and preparation support examination. Excessive scope, personal ranking and missing evidence impair useful findings and constructive participation. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.5 (p. 37); FL-3.2.5 (K1).

questions.prompt: Cases are derived from specified behavior rather than internal decisions. Which family is used?

options.text: Experience-based techniques
Configuration-management techniques
Black-box techniques
White-box techniques

questions.explanation: Specification-derived cases are black-box. Structural derivation is white-box; knowledge of likely faults motivates experience-based work. Configuration management controls versions. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.1 (p. 39); FL-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Integer quantity is rejected below 3, accepted from 3 through 8, and rejected above 8. Which set covers these three partitions?
questions.explanation: 2 covers the lower invalid group, 5 the valid group and 9 the upper invalid group. Each other set misses at least one identified partition. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: An integer score is valid from 20 through 24. Which set achieves full two-value BVA across both partition edges?
questions.explanation: Adjacent cross-partition pairs are 19/20 and 24/25. The alternatives omit boundaries or their immediate neighbors across an edge. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A decision table has eight feasible rules and six have been exercised. What rule coverage has been achieved?
questions.explanation: Coverage is exercised feasible rules divided by total feasible rules: 6/8=75%. Conditions and possible input values are not the denominator. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 (p. 41); FL-4.2.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: Draft --submit--> Pending; Pending --reject--> Draft; Pending --approve--> Approved. Which sequence from Draft covers all three valid transitions?

options.text: submit, reject, submit, reject
submit, submit, reject, approve
submit, reject, submit, approve
submit, approve, reject, submit

questions.explanation: The key follows each stated transition and reaches Approved last. Reject from Approved and submit from Pending are not stated transitions; repeated rejection misses approval. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 (p. 41); FL-4.2.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: A suite executes nine of twelve executable statements. What does the resulting 75% describe?

options.text: Requirements coverage
Defect detection percentage
Decision-rule coverage
Statement coverage

questions.explanation: Nine divided by twelve measures executed statements. Requirements, defects and decision rules are different items with different denominators. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.1 (p. 42); FL-4.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A suite exercises every branch in the executable structure. Which statement is justified?

options.text: It also detects the complete defect population
It also exercises each possible path combination
It also reaches full statement coverage
It also verifies the complete requirement set

questions.explanation: Branch coverage subsumes statement coverage. It does not establish requirements completeness, removal of defects or all combinations of paths. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 (p. 43); FL-4.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A required export format is absent from the implementation. Why can structural coverage miss this omission?

options.text: It measures the code that exists
It measures stakeholder satisfaction
It measures deployed business value
It measures documented acceptance scope

questions.explanation: Structural metrics count implementation items; nonexistent required behavior provides no code item to reach. Specification-derived checks address omissions. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.3 (p. 43); FL-4.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester recalls failures caused by empty filenames and creates related checks. Which technique is illustrated?

options.text: State-model traversal
Error guessing
Decision-table derivation
Branch-based derivation

questions.explanation: The checks arise from experience of likely faults. The other methods require rule combinations, structure or a state model, none of which is the stated basis. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 (p. 43); FL-4.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: In a chartered session, an unexpected response guides the next investigation. Which description fits?

options.text: Design ends before the initial observation
The charter determines each click in advance
Session notes substitute for actual execution
Learning, design and execution evolve together

questions.explanation: Exploratory work adapts further design and execution to observations. It retains a mission and evidence without prescribing every action beforehand. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 (p. 44); FL-4.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A reusable list reminds testers to check interruption, persistence and messages while allowing cases to vary. Which technique fits?

options.text: Decision-table testing
Boundary-value testing
Checklist-based testing
Statement-based testing

questions.explanation: A list of conditions guides checklist-based work. Statements, condition combinations and ordered boundaries are other derivation bases. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 (p. 44); FL-4.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Business staff, a developer and a tester discuss concrete examples for a story. What is the main benefit?

options.text: Shared understanding of desired behavior
Removal of the need for acceptance tests
Automatic calculation of code coverage
A finished implementation design for developers

questions.explanation: Collaborative story writing combines business, development and testing perspectives to create a shared vision of what should be delivered. It does not produce an implementation design, measure code coverage or remove the need for acceptance tests. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 (p. 45); FL-4.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Acceptance criteria list constraints as a checklist rather than Given/When/Then examples. Which style is used?

options.text: Rule-oriented criteria
Scenario-oriented criteria
Implementation branch criteria
Review participation criteria

questions.explanation: Constraints listed as rules are rule-oriented. Scenario-oriented criteria describe situations and outcomes; branch and participation criteria concern other processes. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.2 (p. 45); FL-4.5.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A ticket is refundable when unused and requested at least 48 hours before departure. Which case isolates rejection for prior use?

options.text: Used ticket, requested 30 hours before departure
Unused ticket, requested 60 hours before departure
Used ticket, requested 60 hours before departure
Unused ticket, requested 47 hours before departure

questions.explanation: Used/60 satisfies time and violates usage alone. Unused/47 isolates time, used/30 violates both and unused/60 is accepted. Isolate rules to make failures interpretable. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: Which work product communicates scope, responsibilities, environment needs and completion criteria?

options.text: Test plan
Execution log
Defect report
Coverage trace

questions.explanation: A test plan coordinates objectives, approach and resources. Logs record runs, defect reports describe anomalies and traces link evidence to the basis. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.1 (p. 48); FL-5.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which contribution is appropriate for a tester during iteration planning?

options.text: Split stories into testing tasks and estimate them
Rank the product backlog by business value
Rewrite the organization's test strategy
Approve the release on behalf of the users

questions.explanation: Testers in iteration planning determine testability, break user stories into testing tasks and estimate test effort. Backlog ranking belongs to the product owner, release approval to stakeholders, and the organization's test strategy is not set during an iteration. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.2 (p. 48); FL-5.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: The deadline arrives while important checks remain blocked. What supports an informed completion decision?

options.text: Remove the blocked requirements silently
Substitute historical runs for remaining results
Report unmet criteria and residual risks
Reclassify blocked checks as passed cases

questions.explanation: Decisions need deviations and remaining risk. Changing outcomes, removing scope without disclosure and substituting past evidence misrepresent the current evaluation. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.3 (p. 49); FL-5.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Using E=(O+4M+P)/6 with O=3, M=6 and P=15 days, what is expected effort?

options.text: 7 days
6 days
8 days
12 days

questions.explanation: E=(3+24+15)/6=7 days. Six is the most likely input; eight is the unweighted average; twelve is the range rather than expected effort. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: T1 covers P,Q; T2 covers Q,R,S; T3 covers T,U. T2 is selected. Which remaining test supplies more additional coverage?

options.text: T1 adds two items
T3 adds one item
T1 adds three items
T3 adds two items

questions.explanation: After T2, T1 adds P and T3 adds T,U. Additional coverage excludes already-covered items; total size alone is not the criterion. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: Which distribution reflects the general test-pyramid model?

options.text: One broad check replacing lower-layer checks
Many small isolated checks and fewer broad checks
Many broad UI checks and fewer isolated checks
Equal counts at each layer regardless of cost

questions.explanation: The pyramid favors many fast isolated checks and fewer slower broad checks. Layer names vary; it does not require equal counts or replacement of lower levels. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.6 (p. 50); FL-5.1.6 (K1).

questions.prompt: A session evaluates how real users accomplish tasks with the finished product. Which quadrant fits this business focus and critical purpose?

options.text: Q3
Q1
Q2
