Q4

questions.explanation: Q3 is business-facing and critiques the product. Q2 guides development with business examples; Q1 and Q4 are technology-facing. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.7 (p. 51); FL-5.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which attributes define the assessment of risk level?

options.text: Impact and test effort
Severity and priority
Likelihood and coverage
Likelihood and impact

questions.explanation: Risk level is expressed by risk likelihood and risk impact. Severity and priority classify defects, and test effort and coverage are consequences of risk analysis rather than attributes of the risk. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.1 (p. 52); FL-5.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A specialist leaves, delaying evaluation. Incorrect tax in delivered invoices threatens customers. What are these risks respectively?

options.text: Project risk and product risk
Product risk and project risk
Two configuration risks of the same type
Two review findings rather than risks

questions.explanation: Staff loss threatens schedule, a project concern. Wrong delivered calculations threaten product quality. Related events can still have different risk categories. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.2 (p. 52); FL-5.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Assessment ranks settlement errors above cosmetic issues. Which consequence is appropriate?

options.text: Allocate deeper checks to the financial rules
Defer financial checks until cosmetic work completes
Use equal scope for each item regardless of harm
Allocate effort by the number of screens per feature

questions.explanation: Product risk analysis determines thoroughness, so higher-risk settlement rules receive deeper and earlier testing. Deferring them, allocating effort by screen count or treating all items equally ignores the assessed risk levels. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.3 (p. 52); FL-5.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team adds security checks and then evaluates effectiveness and emerging exposure. Which activities are described?

options.text: Risk mitigation and risk monitoring
Risk identification and staff recruitment
Risk transfer and document archiving
Risk acceptance and schedule cancellation

questions.explanation: Implementing measures mitigates risk; evaluating effectiveness and new exposure monitors risk. The other pairs do not describe these actions. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.4 (p. 53); FL-5.2.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which quantity is a test-progress metric?

options.text: Defect density of the payment component
Number of test cases passed and failed
Average response time of the system
Total cost of testing for the release

questions.explanation: Passed and failed test cases are test progress metrics. Defect density is a defect metric, response time is a product quality metric and the cost of testing is a cost metric. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.1 (p. 54); FL-5.3.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A cycle has ended and stakeholders need achieved objectives, deviations and unresolved issues. Which report fits?

options.text: Environment access request
Test completion report
Daily test progress report
Individual review finding

questions.explanation: Completion reporting consolidates an activity for later decisions. Progress reports support ongoing control; findings and requests have narrower purposes. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.2 (p. 54); FL-5.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A sponsor receives a 95% completion figure while unexecuted cases concern deletion of personal data. What additional information matters most?

options.text: Untested scope and its release implications
The test tools used during execution
A list of testers assigned to each area
The number of test cases executed per day

questions.explanation: Stakeholders need status tailored to their decision, so the untested high-risk scope and its consequences must be explained alongside the percentage. Execution rates, staffing lists and tool names do not show what the missing tests mean for release risk. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.3 (p. 55); FL-5.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Two runs differ after a fixture update. Which record best supports investigation?

options.text: Build, case and data revisions for each run
Defect reports raised during each run
Execution start times for each run
Pass and fail totals for each run

questions.explanation: Configuration management identifies the versions behind a result, so comparing build, test case and data revisions shows what changed. Totals, raised defects and start times describe outcomes or timing, not the configuration that produced them. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.4 (p. 56); FL-5.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A report asserts “the wrong variable caused it” without supporting investigation. Which revision makes the observation actionable?

options.text: Record the suspected variable and omit observed amounts
Record the developer name and request personal discipline
Record a release date and attach an unrelated screenshot
Record inputs, expected amount, actual amount and evidence

questions.explanation: Reproduction conditions, expected and actual outcomes and evidence support triage. Unsupported diagnosis, blame and unrelated attachments impede it; mark suspected causes as hypotheses. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tool flags unreachable code without running the application. Which category fits?

options.text: Static analysis support
Load generation support
Runtime comparison support
Deployment rollback support

questions.explanation: Static analysis inspects structured work products without executing the object. The alternatives concern workload, runtime observations or deployment actions. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.1 (p. 59); FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which benefit can suitable automation provide?

options.text: Elimination of environment configuration effort
Greater repeatability of repeated checks
Removal of expected-result maintenance
Replacement of judgment during exploration

questions.explanation: Automation can improve consistency and reduce repetition. Expected results, human investigation and maintained environments still require work and judgment. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.2 (p. 59); FL-6.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which statement describes a typical test objective?

options.text: Removing the defects found during test execution
Guaranteeing that no failures occur in operation
Defining the processes developers must follow
Checking compliance with legal and regulatory requirements

questions.explanation: Verifying that a test object complies with contractual, legal and regulatory requirements is a typical test objective. Removing defects is debugging, testing cannot guarantee failure-free operation, and defining development processes is a quality-assurance concern. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.1.1 (p. 15); FL-1.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a typical aim of testing?

options.text: Setting the coding standards for developers
Ensuring the required coverage of a test object
Demonstrating that no defects remain after release
Locating and correcting the cause of each failure

questions.explanation: Ensuring the required coverage of a test object is a typical test objective. Locating and correcting causes is debugging, testing cannot demonstrate that no defects remain, and coding standards are set through development or quality-assurance processes. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.1.1 (p. 15); FL-1.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Besides testing, which activity is another form of quality control?

options.text: Training staff on the standard process
Auditing adherence to processes
Defining the development process
Model checking with formal methods

questions.explanation: Testing is a major form of quality control; formal methods such as model checking and proof of correctness, simulation and prototyping are other forms. Defining, auditing and teaching processes are process-oriented quality-assurance activities. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.2 (p. 17); FL-1.2.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: How do testing and quality assurance use test results differently?

options.text: Testing uses them to assess processes; QA to fix defects
Both use them only to make the release decision
QA ignores them because it focuses on products
Testing uses them to fix defects; QA to assess processes

questions.explanation: In testing, results are used to fix defects; in QA they provide feedback on how well the development and test processes are performing. The reversed statement swaps these uses, results serve more than the release decision, and QA is process-oriented rather than product-oriented. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.2 (p. 17); FL-1.2.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which is an advantage of the whole-team approach?

options.text: Higher independence of testing from development
Elimination of acceptance tests by business staff
Better communication and collaboration within the team
Fixed assignment of each task to one specialist

questions.explanation: The whole-team approach improves team dynamics, enhances communication and collaboration, and creates synergy from different skill sets. It reduces rather than increases independence, lets anyone with the skills perform a task, and testers still help business representatives create acceptance tests. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.2 (p. 22); FL-1.5.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: In which situation may the whole-team approach NOT be appropriate?

options.text: A safety-critical product needing high independence
A team where testers coach developers on testing
A co-located team building a web shop
An agile team with business representatives

questions.explanation: The syllabus notes that the whole-team approach may not always be appropriate; for instance, safety-critical contexts can require a high level of test independence. Co-located agile teams with business representatives and testers sharing knowledge are typical settings for the approach. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.2 (p. 22); FL-1.5.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which practice characterizes the whole-team approach?

options.text: Testers alone decide on the automation approach
Business representatives join at final acceptance
Team members share one physical or virtual workspace
Testers work in a separate team that reviews deliverables

questions.explanation: In the whole-team approach team members share the same physical or virtual workspace because co-location eases communication, and testers agree the test strategy and automation approach with developers. A separate reviewing team describes independent testing, and business representatives collaborate throughout, for example on acceptance tests. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.2 (p. 22); FL-1.5.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: A review finds a wrong formula in a requirements document. Which statement about the debugging that follows is correct?

options.text: The defect is removed directly without reproducing a failure
The reviewer must execute the code to locate the defect
Confirmation testing replaces the need to fix the defect
A failure must first be reproduced and then diagnosed

questions.explanation: When static testing finds a defect, debugging is concerned with removing it; reproduction and diagnosis are unnecessary because static testing finds defects directly and cannot cause failures. Reproducing and diagnosing a failure apply to dynamic testing, and confirmation testing checks a fix rather than replacing it. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.1.2 (p. 16); FL-1.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A developer fixes a defect that caused a tester's test to fail. Who should preferably perform the confirmation testing?

options.text: The business representative who accepts releases
The developer who diagnosed and fixed the defect
The tester who ran the original failing test
An independent tester from outside the company

questions.explanation: Confirmation testing checks whether the fix resolved the problem and is preferably done by the same person who performed the initial test. The developer performs debugging, and independent or business testers contribute to other activities and test levels. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.1.2 (p. 16); FL-1.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Involving a representative set of real users throughout development is too costly for a project. How does testing help instead?

options.text: Testers replace the need for user acceptance testing
Testers fix the defects that users would report
Testers guarantee that users will accept the product
Testers keep users' needs in view at every stage

questions.explanation: Testing provides users with indirect representation: testers make sure their understanding of users' needs is considered throughout the lifecycle, because involving real users throughout is usually too expensive. Testers do not replace acceptance testing, defects are fixed through debugging, and testing cannot guarantee acceptance. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.1 (p. 16); FL-1.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Firmware in a medical scanner fails only when exposed to strong electromagnetic fields; its source code was written correctly. What does this illustrate?

options.text: Defects in code cause failures whenever executed
The defect was introduced by an error in the test basis
Root cause analysis cannot apply to hardware effects
Failures can be caused by environmental conditions

questions.explanation: Errors and defects are not the only causes of failures; environmental conditions such as radiation or electromagnetic fields can cause defects in firmware and lead to failures. Not every defect fails whenever executed, the scenario gives no evidence of a test basis error, and root cause analysis can still be performed. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.3 (p. 17); FL-1.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A requirement contains a wrong rule that nobody detects. A designer and a developer then implement it faithfully. What does this illustrate?

options.text: Undetected early defects lead to defective later work products
A defect in code always results in a failure when executed
Defects in documents cannot result in product failures
The developer's implementation is the root cause of the problem

questions.explanation: Defects in work products produced earlier in the lifecycle, if undetected, often lead to defective work products later. Document defects can therefore lead to failures, some code defects fail only under specific conditions, and the faithful implementation is not the fundamental reason for the problem. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.3 (p. 17); FL-1.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A manager asks the team to test every combination of 12 input fields, each with 20 possible values, before release. Which principle explains why the request should be replaced by risk-based selection?

options.text: Tests wear out
Early testing saves time and money
Exhaustive testing is impossible
Defects cluster together

questions.explanation: With 20 to the power of 12 combinations, testing everything is not feasible, so test techniques, prioritization and risk-based testing must focus the effort. Defect clustering, tests wearing out and early testing are valid principles but do not address the infeasibility of the request. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.3 (p. 17); FL-1.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: No failures were found during testing, and a stakeholder claims the software is now proven defect-free. Which principle does this claim ignore?

options.text: A few components contain most of the defects
Testing shows the presence, not the absence, of defects
Testing must be adapted to the context of the product
Verification alone cannot ensure that users' needs are met

questions.explanation: Testing can show that defects are present but cannot prove that none remain; finding no failures only reduces the probability of undiscovered defects. The statement about verification and user needs is the absence-of-defects fallacy, and context dependence and defect clustering do not address the claim. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.3 (p. 17); FL-1.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team reuses the test approach of a casual mobile game for an aircraft flight-control system. Which principle is being ignored?

options.text: Tests wear out
Testing is context dependent
Exhaustive testing is impossible
Defects cluster together

questions.explanation: There is no single universally applicable approach: testing is done differently in different contexts, and a safety-critical flight-control system needs far more rigor than a game. The other principles are valid but do not explain why the approach must change between these contexts. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.3 (p. 17); FL-1.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO statements that correctly reflect the testing principles.

options.text: Predicted defect clusters are an input to risk-based testing
Repeating automated regression tests can still be beneficial
Finding no defects proves the test object is correct
Early testing means later test levels can be skipped
Thorough verification ensures a system meets users' needs

questions.explanation: Although tests wear out, repeating them can be beneficial in automated regression testing, and predicted and observed defect clusters are an important input to risk-based testing. Verification alone does not ensure that user needs are met, early testing does not mean neglecting later testing, and testing cannot prove correctness. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.3 (p. 17); FL-1.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester elaborates test conditions into test cases, identifies coverage items and defines test data and test environment requirements. Which activity is this?

options.text: Test planning
Test analysis
Test design
Test implementation

questions.explanation: Test design elaborates test conditions into test cases, identifies coverage items and defines test data and environment requirements, answering 'how to test'. Test analysis identifies the conditions, implementation creates the testware and environment, and planning sets the objectives and approach. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.1 (p. 18); FL-1.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: At the end of a release, the team creates backlog items for unresolved defects, archives reusable testware and returns the test environment to an agreed state. Which activity is this?

options.text: Test implementation
Test control
Test execution
Test completion

questions.explanation: These are test completion tasks: change requests or backlog items are created for unresolved defects, useful testware is archived or handed over, and the environment is shut down to an agreed state. Control adjusts ongoing work, execution runs tests and implementation prepares testware. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.1 (p. 18); FL-1.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: When analyzing the context of a test process, into which category of contextual factor does 'limited budget and a fixed delivery date' fall?

options.text: Project constraints
Stakeholders
Business domain
Organizational factors

questions.explanation: Scope, time, budget and resources are project constraints. Organizational factors include structure, policies and practices, the business domain covers criticality, risks and regulations, and stakeholder factors concern needs, expectations and cooperation. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.2 (p. 19); FL-1.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which test-related decisions are influenced by contextual factors such as the business domain and technical factors?

options.text: Test strategy, degree of automation and coverage
The quality model of ISO/IEC 25010
The seven testing principles themselves
The definitions of error, defect and failure

questions.explanation: Contextual factors influence many test-related issues, including the test strategy, techniques used, degree of automation, required coverage, level of detail of testware and reporting. Basic definitions, the testing principles and the ISO/IEC 25010 model are general concepts that do not vary with project context. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.2 (p. 19); FL-1.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO work products of test implementation.

options.text: Test logs
Coverage items
A test execution schedule
Test charters
Stubs and drivers

questions.explanation: Test implementation produces test procedures, scripts, suites, test data, the test execution schedule and environment items such as stubs, drivers, simulators and service virtualizations. Test charters and coverage items come from test design, and test logs from test execution. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.3 (p. 20); FL-1.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which work products are typically produced by test analysis?

options.text: Test procedures, test suites and the test data
Prioritized test cases, test charters and coverage items
Test logs and defect reports from executed tests
Prioritized test conditions and test basis defect reports

questions.explanation: Test analysis produces prioritized test conditions, such as acceptance criteria, and defect reports about defects in the test basis. Test cases, charters and coverage items come from test design, procedures and data from implementation, and logs from execution. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.3 (p. 20); FL-1.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Test results are traced to the product risks they address. What does this traceability make possible?

options.text: Calculating statement coverage of the code
Estimating test effort from past ratios
Evaluating the level of residual risk
Determining the root cause of each defect

questions.explanation: Traceability of test results to risks can be used to evaluate the level of residual risk in a test object. Root causes require analysis, statement coverage is measured against the code, and ratio-based estimation uses historical project data. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.4 (p. 20); FL-1.4.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Beyond evaluating coverage, which benefit does good traceability provide?

options.text: It allows tests to run without a test basis
It removes the need for configuration management
It facilitates audits and helps meet IT governance criteria
It automatically sets the priority of each defect

questions.explanation: Good traceability makes it possible to determine the impact of changes, facilitates audits, helps meet IT governance criteria and makes reports easier to understand. It does not replace configuration management, tests still need a basis, and defect priority is a separate decision. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.4 (p. 20); FL-1.4.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: On which test activities does the testing role mainly focus?

options.text: Test analysis, test design, implementation and execution
Test monitoring, design, execution and completion
Test planning, monitoring, control and completion
Test planning, analysis, control and completion

questions.explanation: The testing role takes responsibility for the engineering aspect of testing and focuses on test analysis, design, implementation and execution. Planning, monitoring, control and completion are the focus of the test management role, and the mixed lists combine activities from both roles. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.5 (p. 21); FL-1.4.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester presents a failure to a defensive developer as information about the product, not as a personal attack. Why is this communication skill particularly important for testers?

options.text: Testers should avoid reporting failures to authors
Developers are responsible for communicating all defects
Test results may be perceived as criticism of the author
Good communication replaces the need for defect reports

questions.explanation: Testers are often the bearers of bad news, and test results may be perceived as criticism of the product and its author, so defects should be communicated constructively. Defect reports remain necessary, and testers do report failures rather than avoiding them. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.1 (p. 21); FL-1.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which generic skill most directly increases the efficiency of testing, for example by using appropriate test tools?

options.text: Domain knowledge
Curiosity
Technical knowledge
Active listening

questions.explanation: The syllabus links technical knowledge to the efficiency of testing, for example through appropriate test tools. Domain knowledge helps in understanding and communicating with business representatives, active listening supports interaction, and curiosity helps to find hard-to-find defects. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.1 (p. 21); FL-1.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A company moves all testing to an external test team. Which drawback of this independence is most likely?

options.text: Testers will share the developers' assumptions and biases
Fewer kinds of failures will be recognized
Developers may lose their sense of responsibility for quality
Testers will become too familiar with the code

questions.explanation: A drawback of independent testing is that developers may lose a sense of responsibility for quality, and isolation can harm communication. Independent testers are less likely to share the authors' biases and tend to recognize different kinds of failures, which are benefits. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.3 (p. 22); FL-1.5.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which is a good testing practice in any SDLC?

options.text: Every development activity has a corresponding test activity
All test levels share the same test objectives
Test design for each level starts after its code is complete
Testers review work products after final approval

questions.explanation: For every software development activity there should be a corresponding test activity, so that all development activities are subject to quality control. Test analysis and design start during the corresponding development phase, levels have different objectives, and testers review drafts as soon as they are available. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.2 (p. 25); FL-2.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: According to good testing practices, when should test analysis and design for a given test level begin?

options.text: When the test object is ready for execution
During the corresponding development phase
At the start of test completion
After the previous test level is complete

questions.explanation: Test analysis and design for a test level begin during the corresponding development phase, so that testing adheres to the principle of early testing. Waiting for the previous level, an executable object or test completion delays feedback. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.2 (p. 25); FL-2.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Testers review work products as soon as drafts are available. Which approach does this good practice support?

options.text: Testing quadrants
Test pyramid
Exhaustive testing
Shift left

questions.explanation: Involving testers in reviewing drafts enables earlier testing and defect detection, which supports shift left. The test pyramid concerns test granularity, exhaustive testing is impossible, and the quadrants group test types and levels. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.2 (p. 25); FL-2.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which approach typically expresses test cases in a Given/When/Then format that stakeholders can easily understand?

options.text: Behavior-driven development
Feature-driven development
Domain-driven design
Test-driven development

questions.explanation: BDD expresses desired behavior with test cases written in simple natural language, usually in the Given/When/Then format, which are then translated into executable tests. TDD directs coding through tests, while domain-driven design and feature-driven development are not test-first approaches. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.3 (p. 26); FL-2.1.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: What do TDD, ATDD and BDD have in common?

options.text: Tests are executed only after system integration
Tests are written by an independent test team
Tests are derived from the code's internal structure
Tests are defined before the code is written

questions.explanation: In TDD, ATDD and BDD tests are defined before the code is written, so they implement early testing and shift left. They are not structure-based, are not reserved for an independent team, and provide feedback long before system integration. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.3 (p. 26); FL-2.1.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: In TDD, ATDD and BDD, what can happen to the test cases after the code has been written?

options.text: They are converted into exploratory test charters
They may persist as automated tests for future changes
They replace the need for regression testing
They are discarded once the code passes them

questions.explanation: For all three approaches, tests may persist as automated tests to ensure code quality in future adaptations and refactoring. Discarding them loses this value, they are not turned into charters, and they become part of regression testing rather than replacing it. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.3 (p. 26); FL-2.1.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: Before taking over a new system, system administrators check backup, restore and disaster recovery procedures. Which form of acceptance testing is this?

options.text: User acceptance testing
Contractual acceptance testing
Regulatory acceptance testing
Operational acceptance testing

questions.explanation: Checking backup, restore and recovery from the operators' perspective is operational acceptance testing. User acceptance testing checks business use by intended users, contractual testing checks contract criteria, and regulatory testing checks compliance with regulations. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.1 (p. 28); FL-2.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Components are integrated one at a time, starting with the lowest-level modules and using drivers to call them. Which integration strategy does this component integration testing follow?

options.text: Bottom-up
Big-bang
Top-down
Risk-based

questions.explanation: Starting from the lowest-level components and using drivers to call them is bottom-up integration. Top-down starts from the highest level and uses stubs, big-bang integrates everything at once, and risk-based testing is a test approach rather than an integration strategy. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.1 (p. 28); FL-2.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A product is released to a limited group of existing customers who use it at their own sites before general release. Which form of acceptance testing is this?

options.text: Alpha testing
System integration testing
Beta testing
Operational acceptance testing

questions.explanation: Beta testing is performed by potential or existing customers at their own locations. Alpha testing takes place at the developing organization's site, operational acceptance testing focuses on operations, and system integration testing checks interfaces to other systems. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.1 (p. 28); FL-2.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester checks that an insurance quote calculates the specified premium for each pricing rule. Which main objective of functional testing does this address?

options.text: Functional appropriateness
Compatibility
Performance efficiency
Functional correctness

questions.explanation: Checking that functions produce the specified results addresses functional correctness, one of the main objectives of functional testing alongside completeness and appropriateness. Appropriateness concerns how well functions facilitate tasks, and performance efficiency and compatibility are non-functional characteristics. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.2 (p. 29); FL-2.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: An application must run unchanged on two different operating systems. Which ISO/IEC 25010 quality characteristic does testing this concern?

options.text: Compatibility
Maintainability
Portability
Reliability

questions.explanation: Being transferable to another platform is portability, also called flexibility. Compatibility concerns co-existence and information exchange with other systems, reliability concerns failure-free operation, and maintainability concerns ease of modification. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.2 (p. 29); FL-2.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement about the four test types described in the syllabus is correct?

options.text: White-box testing applies only at component level
All four can be applied at every test level
Black-box testing cannot be used for acceptance
Non-functional testing must wait for system testing

questions.explanation: Functional, non-functional, black-box and white-box testing can all be applied at all test levels, although the focus differs. White-box testing is also used at higher levels, non-functional testing can start early, and black-box testing is common in acceptance testing. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.2 (p. 29); FL-2.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Before running regression tests after a change, what is advisable in order to recognize the extent of regression testing?

options.text: Holding a retrospective
Performing an impact analysis
Repeating the confirmation test
Calculating the defect density

questions.explanation: Impact analysis shows which parts of the software could be affected by a change, so it helps to decide the extent of regression testing. A confirmation test checks only the fix, retrospectives review the process, and defect density is a defect metric. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.3 (p. 30); FL-2.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A legacy order system is replaced, and its customer data is moved into the maintained application. Which maintenance testing activity is especially needed?

options.text: Usability testing of the old user interface
Confirmation testing of old defect fixes
Testing the conversion of the migrated data
Static analysis of the legacy source code

questions.explanation: When data from another application is migrated into the system being maintained, tests of data conversion are needed alongside tests of the changed environment. Analyzing legacy code, testing the old interface or re-confirming old fixes does not check that the migrated data is correct. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.3 (p. 31); FL-2.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: On which factors does the scope of maintenance testing typically depend?

options.text: Age of the system, team location and release name
Risk of the change, size of the system and size of the change
Number of testers, tool licences and test levels
Defect density, review type and coverage tool

questions.explanation: The scope of maintenance testing typically depends on the degree of risk of the change, the size of the existing system and the size of the change. Staffing, tooling, team location and review types do not define that scope. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.3 (p. 31); FL-2.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: In an agile project where change is expected throughout, which testing characteristic is typically favored?

options.text: Lightweight documentation and extensive test automation
Detailed test documentation written before coding
Dynamic testing after all code is complete
Mostly scripted manual tests from full specifications

questions.explanation: Agile development favors lightweight work product documentation and extensive automation to make regression testing easier, with most manual testing using experience-based techniques. Detailed upfront documentation, late dynamic testing and fully scripted manual tests fit sequential models better. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.1 (p. 25); FL-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: In a sequential development model, why does dynamic testing typically start late in the lifecycle?

options.text: Executable code is usually created in later phases
Regression testing is performed in each iteration
Testers are not allowed to review requirements
Test levels are combined into a single phase

questions.explanation: In sequential models, executable code usually appears in later phases, so early tester involvement focuses on requirement reviews, test analysis and test design. Testers do review requirements, test levels remain separate, and regression testing in each iteration describes iterative models. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.1 (p. 25); FL-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team holds a retrospective at the end of an iteration. Select TWO topics that are typically discussed.

options.text: Whether to cancel the remaining test levels
What was successful and should be retained
Which user stories to commit to next
What was not successful and could be improved
Which team member caused the most defects

questions.explanation: Retrospective participants discuss what was successful and should be retained, what could be improved, and how to incorporate improvements; results are normally recorded in the test completion report. Blaming individuals is not an objective, and selecting stories belongs to iteration planning. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.6 (p. 28); FL-2.1.6 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO risks or challenges of DevOps from a testing perspective.

options.text: Regression risk grows with the number of automated tests
Feedback on code quality becomes slower
Visibility of non-functional characteristics decreases
The delivery pipeline must be defined and established
CI/CD tools must be introduced and maintained

questions.explanation: DevOps risks include the need to define and establish the delivery pipeline, to introduce and maintain CI/CD tools, and to resource test automation. DevOps speeds up feedback, increases the visibility of non-functional characteristics and minimizes regression risk through automated regression tests. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.4 (p. 26); FL-2.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team adopts DevOps with a high level of automated testing. Which statement about manual testing is correct?

options.text: It replaces automated regression testing in pipelines
It should be limited to static analysis of code
It is no longer needed once pipelines run the tests
It is still needed, especially from the user's perspective

questions.explanation: Although DevOps comes with a high level of automated testing, manual testing, especially from the user's perspective, is still needed. Static analysis is a tool-supported technique, and manual testing complements rather than replaces automated regression tests. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.4 (p. 26); FL-2.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which practice is an example of shift left?

options.text: Postponing reviews until the system test basis is final
Performing non-functional testing at component level
Starting test design after code integration
Running performance tests on the complete system alone

questions.explanation: Performing non-functional testing starting at the component test level, where possible, is a form of shift left. Postponing reviews, testing performance only on the complete system and designing tests after integration all move testing later. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.5 (p. 27); FL-2.1.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: A manager objects that shift left adds training and effort early in a project. Which response reflects the syllabus?

options.text: Shift left means later testing can be neglected
Shift left requires no stakeholder agreement
Early effort can be avoided by skipping reviews
Early costs are expected to save effort and cost later

questions.explanation: Shift left might cause extra training, effort or costs earlier but is expected to save effort and costs later, and stakeholders need to be convinced of the concept. It does not mean neglecting later testing, and reviews are a key shift-left practice. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.5 (p. 27); FL-2.1.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which work product is NOT appropriate for static testing?

options.text: An exploratory session's test charter
A state model of the ordering system
Licensed third-party executable code
The supplier contract for the project

questions.explanation: Almost any work product can be examined statically, including test charters, contracts and models. Work products that are difficult for people to interpret and should not be analyzed by tools, such as third-party executable code for legal reasons, are not appropriate. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.1 (p. 33); FL-3.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which condition allows a work product to be checked by static analysis as well as by review?

options.text: It has been approved by the product owner
It has been executed at least once in a test environment
It is shorter than an agreed page limit
It has a checkable structure, such as formal syntax

questions.explanation: Any readable work product can be reviewed, but static analysis needs a structure to check against, such as models, code or text with a formal syntax. Execution is not needed for static analysis, and approval or document length do not make a work product analyzable by tools. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.1 (p. 33); FL-3.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: What can result when stakeholders are rarely involved during the SDLC?

options.text: Earlier detection of quality problems
Costly rework and missed deadlines
Fewer changes to the requirements
Faster agreement on acceptance criteria

questions.explanation: With little stakeholder involvement, the product might not meet their original or current vision, which can cause costly rework, missed deadlines, blame games and even project failure. Little involvement does not reduce requirement changes but hides them until late, and faster agreement and earlier detection of quality problems come from frequent feedback. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.1 (p. 35); FL-3.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which review role takes overall responsibility for the review, such as deciding who is involved and organizing when and where it takes place?

options.text: Review leader
Reviewer
Moderator
Manager

questions.explanation: The review leader takes overall responsibility for the review, deciding who will be involved and organizing when and where it takes place. The moderator runs review meetings, the manager decides what is reviewed and provides resources, and reviewers perform the review. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.3 (p. 36); FL-3.2.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: In a review, who decides what is to be reviewed and provides resources such as staff and time?

options.text: Review leader
Moderator
Manager
Author

questions.explanation: The manager decides what is to be reviewed and provides resources such as staff and time. The review leader organizes the review, the moderator facilitates meetings, and the author creates and fixes the work product. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.3 (p. 36); FL-3.2.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which responsibility belongs to the author in a review?

options.text: Creating and fixing the work product under review
Deciding who will take part in the review
Collating anomalies and recording decisions
Ensuring a safe environment in which everyone speaks freely

questions.explanation: The author creates the work product and fixes it after the review. The moderator ensures a safe environment and effective meetings, the scribe collates anomalies and records decisions, and the review leader decides who takes part. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.3 (p. 36); FL-3.2.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which factor contributes to a successful review?

options.text: Skipping training because roles are intuitive
Evaluating participants' performance as an objective
Support from management for the review process
Reviewing the whole document in one long session

questions.explanation: Management support for the review process is a success factor, as are clear objectives, small chunks, adequate preparation time and training. Evaluating participants should never be an objective, long sessions reduce concentration, and participants need training to fulfil their roles. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.5 (p. 37); FL-3.2.5 (K1).

questions.prompt: Reviews in a company often fail because participants do not know what their roles require. Which success factor addresses this?

options.text: Making evaluation of participants an objective
Reviewing larger chunks in each session
Shortening the preparation time
Providing adequate training for all participants

questions.explanation: Adequate training lets all participants know how to fulfil their roles, which is one of the listed review success factors. Larger chunks reduce concentration, evaluating participants should never be an objective, and participants need adequate preparation time. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.5 (p. 37); FL-3.2.5 (K1).

questions.prompt: Select TWO defects that are typically easier and cheaper to find through static testing than through dynamic testing.

options.text: A variable that is used before it is declared
An incorrect total shown in a running report
A crash on one specific device model
A slow response time under peak load
A mismatch in the number of interface parameters

questions.explanation: Incorrect interface specifications, such as a mismatched number, type or order of parameters, and coding defects such as undeclared variables are typical static testing findings. Response times, device-specific crashes and wrong displayed totals are failures observed by executing the software. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.3 (p. 34); FL-3.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Static analysis identifies unreachable code. Why is this a particular value of static testing?

options.text: Dynamic tests cannot reveal such defects
It proves that the remaining code is defect-free
It measures how fast the code executes
It replaces the need for code reviews

questions.explanation: Static testing can identify defects that dynamic testing cannot detect, such as unreachable code, design patterns not implemented as desired and defects in non-executable work products. It does not prove correctness, measure execution speed or make reviews unnecessary. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.2 (p. 33); FL-3.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which quality characteristic can static testing measure because it is independent of code execution?

options.text: Response time under load
Reliability in operation
Performance efficiency
Maintainability

questions.explanation: Static testing can measure quality characteristics that do not depend on executing code, such as maintainability. Dynamic testing measures execution-dependent characteristics such as performance efficiency, reliability and response time. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.3 (p. 34); FL-3.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A review is led by a moderator, uses qualified engineers as reviewers and aims to gain consensus and decide on an engineering problem. Which review type is this?

options.text: Informal review
Walkthrough
Inspection
Technical review

questions.explanation: A technical review is performed by technically qualified reviewers, led by a moderator, and aims to gain consensus and make decisions on a technical problem. Walkthroughs are led by the author, inspections focus on finding the maximum number of anomalies, and informal reviews follow no defined process. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.4 (p. 36); FL-3.2.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: In which review type may the author NOT act as the review leader or scribe?

options.text: Inspection
Technical review
Informal review
Walkthrough

questions.explanation: Inspections are the most formal review type: they follow the complete generic process, collect metrics, and do not allow the author to act as review leader or scribe. In a walkthrough the author leads, and technical and informal reviews have no such restriction. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.4 (p. 36); FL-3.2.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: During which review activity are the scope, quality characteristics to evaluate, exit criteria and timeframes defined?

options.text: Individual review
Planning
Review initiation
Communication and analysis

questions.explanation: During planning, the scope of the review is defined, including its purpose, the work product, quality characteristics, focus areas, exit criteria, supporting information, effort and timeframes. Initiation prepares participants, individual review finds anomalies, and communication and analysis discusses them. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.2 (p. 35); FL-3.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Participants are given access to the work product, understand their roles and receive everything they need. Which review activity is this?

options.text: Planning
Fixing and reporting
Review initiation
Individual review

questions.explanation: Review initiation makes sure everyone and everything involved is prepared to start: access to the work product, understanding of roles and the necessary materials. Planning defines scope and criteria, individual review assesses the work product, and fixing and reporting follows up defects. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.2 (p. 35); FL-3.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why do black-box test cases often remain useful when the implementation changes?

options.text: They rely on the tester's experience of past failures
They are generated from the code's control flow
They do not depend on how the software is built
They are executed only at component level

questions.explanation: Black-box test cases are based on the specified behavior without reference to internal structure, so they remain useful if the implementation changes but the required behavior stays the same. Control flow is a white-box basis, past failures drive experience-based techniques, and black-box tests are used at all levels. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.1 (p. 39); FL-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: When can white-box test cases be created?

options.text: Independently of how the software is designed
Only when specifications are complete and detailed
Only after the design or implementation exists
Before any requirements have been written

questions.explanation: White-box test cases depend on how the software is designed, so they can only be created after the design or implementation of the test object. They are not independent of the design, and they are useful even when specifications are vague or incomplete. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.1 (p. 39); FL-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: What is the main reason for using experience-based techniques alongside black-box and white-box techniques?

options.text: They derive tests from formal models of behavior
They give a measurable code coverage figure
They can find defects that the other families miss
They need no tester skills to be effective

questions.explanation: Experience-based techniques use testers' knowledge and can detect defects missed by black-box and white-box techniques, so they are complementary. They do not measure code coverage, their effectiveness depends heavily on tester skills, and formal models are a black-box basis. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.1 (p. 39); FL-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt:
Consider the following code:
READ amount, member
discount = 0
IF amount > 100 THEN
    discount = 10
ENDIF
IF member THEN
    discount = discount + 5
ENDIF
PRINT discount
What is the minimum number of test cases needed to achieve 100% statement coverage?
questions.explanation: One test with an amount above 100 and a member executes every executable statement, including both assignments inside the IF statements. Statement coverage does not require the false outcomes of the decisions, which branch coverage would need. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.1 (p. 42); FL-4.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A function reaches 100% statement coverage, yet later fails when a denominator is zero. What explains why the tests missed this?

options.text: The division statement was never executed by the tests
Statement coverage measures requirements, not code
100% statement coverage includes all branches
Statement coverage does not detect data-dependent defects

questions.explanation: Exercising a statement does not detect every defect: data-dependent defects such as division by zero fail only for particular values. With 100% statement coverage the division did execute, statement coverage does not ensure that all branches are taken, and it measures executable statements in the code. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.1 (p. 42); FL-4.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt:
Consider the following code:
READ x
IF x > 0 THEN
    PRINT "positive"
ENDIF
WHILE x > 10 DO
    x = x - 10
ENDWHILE
PRINT x
Test 1 uses x = 25. Which additional test achieves 100% branch coverage together with test 1?
questions.explanation: With x = 25 the IF decision is true and the loop both repeats and exits, so only the false outcome of the IF is missing; any x of 0 or less, such as 0, takes it. The values 5, 15 and 30 are positive and repeat outcomes already covered. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 (p. 43); FL-4.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement about branch coverage is correct?

options.text: It includes unconditional as well as conditional branches
It counts the true outcome of each decision
Full statement coverage implies full branch coverage
It requires executing each possible path in the code

questions.explanation: A branch is a transfer of control between two nodes in the control flow graph, either unconditional (straight-line code) or conditional (a decision outcome), and branch coverage counts both. False outcomes count too, statement coverage does not imply branch coverage, and branch coverage does not require every path. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 (p. 43); FL-4.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt:
Consider the following code:
READ a, b
IF a > b THEN
    PRINT a
ELSE
    PRINT b
ENDIF
IF a = 0 THEN
    PRINT "zero"
ENDIF
What is the minimum number of test cases needed to achieve 100% branch coverage?
questions.explanation: Two tests suffice: for example a = 0, b = -1 takes the true outcome of both decisions, and a = 1, b = 5 takes both false outcomes. One test cannot take both outcomes of the same decision, and three or four tests are more than the minimum. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 (p. 43); FL-4.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which is a strength of white-box testing?

options.text: It replaces the need for black-box test techniques
It can find defects even when the specification is vague
It reliably detects requirements that were never implemented
It needs no access to the code or design

questions.explanation: Because the entire implementation is taken into account, white-box testing facilitates defect detection even when the specification is vague, outdated or incomplete. Its weakness is that it may not detect defects of omission; it requires knowledge of the internal structure and complements black-box techniques. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.3 (p. 43); FL-4.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: How can white-box test techniques be used in static testing?

options.text: By executing the code under peak load conditions
By replacing pseudocode reviews with test runs
Only by measuring coverage with an execution tool
In dry runs of code that is not yet ready to execute

questions.explanation: White-box techniques can be used statically, for example in dry runs of code not yet ready for execution, and are well suited to reviewing pseudocode and other logic that can be modeled as a control flow graph. Coverage tools and load conditions involve execution. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.3 (p. 43); FL-4.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester builds a list of possible errors, defects and failures and designs tests to expose each one. What is this way of implementing error guessing called?

options.text: Fault attack
Session-based testing
Defect clustering
Checklist-based review

questions.explanation: Fault attacks implement error guessing: the tester creates or acquires a list of possible errors, defects and failures and designs tests that expose the defects or cause the failures. Session-based testing structures exploratory testing, and defect clustering is a testing principle. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 (p. 43); FL-4.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester anticipates that developers often use the wrong comparison operator in loop conditions. To which error category in the syllabus does this belong?

options.text: Data
Logic
Input
Interfaces

questions.explanation: The syllabus groups errors by area; a wrong operator or a missing case is a logic error. Input errors concern accepting or rejecting inputs, interface errors concern parameter mismatches and incompatible types, and data errors concern initialization or types. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 (p. 43); FL-4.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: In which situation is exploratory testing particularly useful?

options.text: When regulators require fully scripted evidence
When specifications are inadequate and time is short
When tests must be repeated identically each night
When the tester has little domain knowledge

questions.explanation: Exploratory testing is useful when there are few or inadequate specifications or significant time pressure, and to complement more formal techniques. Scripted evidence and identical nightly runs favor scripted or automated tests, and exploratory testing works best with experienced testers who have domain knowledge. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 (p. 44); FL-4.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: In session-based exploratory testing, what typically follows the time-boxed session?

options.text: A debriefing with interested stakeholders
A static analysis of the session sheets
A three-point estimate of the session
A formal inspection of the test charter

questions.explanation: The test session is usually followed by a debriefing between the tester and stakeholders interested in the results. The charter guides the session rather than being inspected afterwards, and estimation and static analysis are unrelated activities. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 (p. 44); FL-4.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which item is suitable for inclusion in a test checklist?

options.text: Is an error shown when a mandatory field is empty?
Is the software of good quality for its users?
Have all exit criteria for system testing been met?
Does the source code compile without any warnings?

questions.explanation: Checklist items are often phrased as questions that can be checked separately and directly. Items that can be checked automatically, items better suited as entry or exit criteria, and items that are too general should not be included. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 (p. 44); FL-4.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why should checklists be updated regularly based on defect analysis?

options.text: Updating makes test results fully repeatable
Checklist items must be checked automatically
Longer checklists give better coverage
Entries lose effect as developers learn to avoid errors

questions.explanation: Some entries become less effective over time because developers learn to avoid the same errors, and new entries may be needed for newly found high-severity defects. Checklists should not grow too long, should not contain automatically checkable items, and high-level checklists reduce repeatability. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 (p. 44); FL-4.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: What are the three critical aspects of a user story, known as the 3 C's?

options.text: Customer, Code, Confirmation
Context, Conversation, Completion
Card, Conversation, Confirmation
Card, Criteria, Coverage

questions.explanation: A user story has three critical aspects: the Card (the medium describing it), the Conversation (explaining how the software will be used) and the Confirmation (the acceptance criteria). The other lists mix in unrelated terms. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 (p. 45); FL-4.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: During refinement, a stakeholder cannot say how a user story would be tested. According to INVEST, what might this indicate?

options.text: The story may be unclear or lack value to them
The story must be implemented before testing
The story is independent of other stories
The story is too small to be estimated

questions.explanation: Good stories are Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable. If a stakeholder does not know how to test a story, it may not be clear enough, may not reflect something valuable to them, or they may just need help in testing. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 (p. 45); FL-4.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO purposes of acceptance criteria.

options.text: Specifying the internal design of the code
Defining the scope of the user story
Allowing accurate planning and estimation
Measuring branch coverage of the story
Replacing the conversation with stakeholders

questions.explanation: Acceptance criteria define the scope of the story, help reach consensus, describe positive and negative scenarios, serve as a basis for acceptance testing and allow accurate planning and estimation. They do not specify internal design, they result from the conversation, and they are not a code coverage measure. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.2 (p. 45); FL-4.5.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A booking form has three inputs: seat class (economy, business, first), meal (standard, vegetarian) and payment (card, voucher, invoice, points). Each value forms one partition and all combinations are valid. What is the minimum number of test cases for Each Choice coverage?
questions.explanation: Each Choice coverage requires each partition of each input to be exercised at least once, and one test can cover a partition from every input. The largest set has four payment partitions, so four tests are needed; 24 would be all combinations. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A password length is valid from 8 to 16 characters. Lengths from 0 to 7 and from 17 upwards are invalid. Tests use lengths 10, 12 and 20. What equivalence partition coverage is achieved?
questions.explanation: There are three partitions: 0 to 7 (invalid), 8 to 16 (valid) and 17 or more (invalid). Tests 10 and 12 exercise the same valid partition and 20 the upper invalid one, so two of three partitions are covered, about 67%. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A loyalty scheme assigns discounts by customer type: student and senior receive 10%, staff receives 20% and standard receives none. Any other type is rejected. Assuming types with the same discount are processed the same way, how many equivalence partitions does customer type have?
questions.explanation: Values processed the same way form one partition: student and senior (10%), staff (20%), standard (no discount), plus the invalid partition for any other type, giving four. Counting student and senior separately gives five; omitting the invalid partition gives three. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: An integer quantity is accepted from 1 to 50 inclusive; values below 1 and above 50 are rejected. Which set of test values achieves 100% coverage with 3-value boundary value analysis?
questions.explanation: The boundary values are 0 and 1 at the lower edge and 50 and 51 at the upper edge. 3-value BVA adds both neighbors of each boundary value, giving -1, 0, 1, 2 and 49, 50, 51, 52. Using only the valid boundaries 1 and 50 gives six values and misses -1 and 52. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A field accepts integers from 10 to 20; other values are rejected. Using 2-value boundary value analysis, tests use 9, 10 and 15. What boundary value coverage is achieved?
questions.explanation: With 2-value BVA the coverage items are the boundary values 9, 10, 20 and 21. Tests 9 and 10 exercise two of them, and 15 is not a boundary value, so coverage is 2/4 = 50%. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A requirement states that integer values of x of 50 or more are accepted. The code is wrongly implemented as 'IF x = 50 THEN accept'. Which test value, added by 3-value boundary value analysis to the 2-value set, detects this defect?
questions.explanation: 2-value BVA tests 49 and 50, which the faulty code handles correctly. 3-value BVA adds 48 and 51; for 51 the requirement accepts but 'x = 50' rejects, so the defect is revealed. 48 is rejected by both versions. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: Integer ages are classified as child (0 to 12), teenager (13 to 17) or adult (18 to 120); all other values are invalid. Using 2-value boundary value analysis, how many coverage items are there?
questions.explanation: The partition edges lie between -1 and 0, 12 and 13, 17 and 18, and 120 and 121, giving eight boundary values, each of which is a 2-value coverage item. Six omits the invalid partitions' boundaries, and 16 is the number of 3-value coverage items. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A decision table has three Boolean conditions: registered customer, order above 100 and express delivery. Express delivery is available to registered customers alone. How many columns remain after removing infeasible combinations from the full table?
questions.explanation: Three Boolean conditions give 2^3 = 8 combinations. Express delivery without registration is infeasible for both values of the order condition, which removes two columns and leaves six feasible rules. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 (p. 41); FL-4.2.3 (K3).

questions.prompt:
A minimized decision table for loans ('–' means the condition is irrelevant):
R1: Employed = F → Reject
R2: Employed = T, Income above 3000 = F, Existing debt = – → Reject
R3: Employed = T, Income above 3000 = T, Existing debt = T → Refer to a manager
R4: Employed = T, Income above 3000 = T, Existing debt = F → Grant the loan
Which action is expected for an employed applicant with an income of 2500 and no existing debt?

options.text: No rule matches, so reject by default
Refer to a manager
Grant the loan
Reject

questions.explanation: An employed applicant with an income of 2500 has 'Income above 3000 = F', which matches R2, where existing debt is irrelevant. The action is to reject because R2 matches, not by default. Granting applies only to R4, which requires income above 3000 and no existing debt. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 (p. 41); FL-4.2.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: A full decision table has four Boolean conditions, and two of its combinations are infeasible. Tests exercise 7 of the feasible columns. What decision table coverage is achieved?
questions.explanation: Coverage items are the feasible columns: 2^4 = 16 combinations minus 2 infeasible ones gives 14. Exercising 7 of 14 gives 50%. Dividing by all 16 columns, about 44%, wrongly counts the infeasible combinations. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 (p. 41); FL-4.2.3 (K3).

questions.prompt:
Requirements for a shop's discounts:
- Customers over 65 receive a 10% senior discount.
- Loyalty-card holders receive a 5% loyalty discount.
- One discount can be applied per order.
While building a decision table from these rules, which combination reveals a gap in the requirements?

options.text: A loyalty-card holder over 65
A loyalty-card holder aged 40
A customer over 65 without a card
A customer aged 30 without a card

questions.explanation: Enumerating the combinations shows that a card holder over 65 qualifies for both discounts, but the requirements do not say which single discount applies. Each of the other combinations qualifies for at most one discount, so its outcome is defined. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 (p. 41); FL-4.2.3 (K3).

questions.prompt:
A media player has the states Stopped, Playing and Paused, and the events play, pause and stop. Its valid transitions are:
Stopped --play--> Playing
Playing --pause--> Paused
Playing --stop--> Stopped
Paused --play--> Playing
Paused --stop--> Stopped
All other state and event combinations are invalid. How many coverage items does all transitions coverage have?
questions.explanation: In all transitions coverage the coverage items are all transitions in the state table, valid and invalid: 3 states × 3 events = 9 cells, of which 5 are valid and 4 invalid. Five is the number of items for valid transitions coverage, and three is the number of states. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 (p. 41); FL-4.2.4 (K3).

questions.prompt:
A document workflow starts in Draft. Its valid transitions are:
Draft --submit--> Review
Review --approve--> Published
Review --reject--> Draft
Published --archive--> Archived
Archived is a final state, and each test case starts in Draft. What is the minimum number of test cases for 100% valid transitions coverage?
questions.explanation: A single sequence submit, reject, submit, approve, archive exercises all four valid transitions, because one test case can cover several transitions. Separate tests for the reject and approve paths are not needed since reject returns to Draft. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 (p. 41); FL-4.2.4 (K3).

questions.prompt:
A login model labels transitions as 'event [guard] / action':
LoggedOut --login [valid password] / open session--> LoggedIn
LoggedOut --login [invalid password and failures < 2] / count failure--> LoggedOut
LoggedOut --login [invalid password and failures = 2] / lock account--> Locked
LoggedIn --logout / close session--> LoggedOut
In state LoggedOut with 2 previous failures, the user logs in with an invalid password. Which result is expected?

options.text: Locked, with the account locked
LoggedIn, with a session opened
LoggedOut, with the failure counted
LoggedOut, with the account locked

questions.explanation: The event login with an invalid password and two previous failures satisfies the guard [invalid password and failures = 2], so the transition locks the account and moves to Locked. Counting another failure requires fewer than two previous failures. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 (p. 41); FL-4.2.4 (K3).

questions.prompt:
A ticket has these valid transitions:
New --assign--> Open
Open --resolve--> Resolved
Resolved --reopen--> Open
Resolved --close--> Closed
Open --cancel--> Closed
A test starting in New performs assign, resolve, close. What valid transitions coverage does it achieve?
questions.explanation: The test exercises assign, resolve and close, three of the five valid transitions, so valid transitions coverage is 60%. It visits all four states, so 100% would be its all states coverage, which is a weaker criterion. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 (p. 41); FL-4.2.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team uses ATDD for the story 'As a shopper, I want to save my cart so that I can finish the purchase later'. In which order are the test cases typically written?

options.text: Positive cases, then non-functional cases, then negative cases
Non-functional cases, then positive cases, then negative cases
Positive cases, then negative cases, then non-functional cases
Negative cases, then positive cases, then non-functional cases

questions.explanation: In ATDD the first test cases are typically positive, confirming correct behavior without exceptions or error conditions. Negative testing follows, and finally the team covers non-functional quality characteristics such as performance efficiency or usability. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: Story: As a library member, I want to borrow books so that I can read them at home. Acceptance criteria: a member may hold at most 5 books at a time; a member with an overdue book cannot borrow. Which test case is an appropriate negative test derived from these criteria?

options.text: Member with 2 books borrows an e-book from a partner library; expect refusal
Member with 4 books and none overdue borrows a fifth; expect success
Member with 5 books and none overdue borrows a sixth; expect success
Member with 5 books and none overdue borrows a sixth; expect refusal

questions.explanation: A negative test checks behavior that the criteria forbid: a member holding five books must be refused a sixth. Borrowing a fifth book is a positive test, expecting success at the limit contradicts the criterion, and partner-library e-books go beyond the story. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: Acceptance criteria for a password reset story: (1) a reset link is emailed to a registered address; (2) the link expires after 30 minutes. Select TWO proposed test cases that should NOT be part of this story's ATDD tests.

options.text: The new password must have at least 12 characters
An account locks after three failed logins
A password reset link reaches a registered address
A link used after 31 minutes is rejected
A link used after 29 minutes is accepted

questions.explanation: ATDD test cases must cover all characteristics of the user story and should not go beyond it. Password length rules and account locking are not part of these acceptance criteria, whereas the link delivery and the 29- and 31-minute cases check the stated criteria. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: Which tester contribution belongs to release planning rather than iteration planning?

options.text: Breaking user stories into testing tasks
Estimating effort for each testing task
Defining the test approach across all iterations
Assessing testability of iteration backlog stories

questions.explanation: In release planning testers write testable stories and acceptance criteria, take part in risk analyses, estimate effort for stories, determine the test approach and plan testing for the release. Breaking stories into tasks, estimating task effort and assessing testability of the iteration backlog belong to iteration planning. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.2 (p. 48); FL-5.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: During release planning, which contribution do testers typically make?

options.text: Approving the release budget for the project
Ranking the product backlog by business value
Writing testable user stories and acceptance criteria
Fixing defects found in the previous release

questions.explanation: Testers involved in release planning participate in writing testable user stories and acceptance criteria, risk analyses, estimation and planning the test approach. Fixing defects is debugging, budget approval is a management decision and backlog ranking belongs to the product owner. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.2 (p. 48); FL-5.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which is an example of a product quality metric?

options.text: Defect detection percentage
Mean time to failure
Cost of testing
Test case implementation progress

questions.explanation: Product quality metrics include availability, response time and mean time to failure. Implementation progress is a test progress metric, defect detection percentage is a defect metric and cost of testing is a cost metric. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.1 (p. 54); FL-5.3.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a risk metric?

options.text: Test execution time
Residual risk level
Defect density
Requirements coverage

questions.explanation: Residual risk level is listed as a risk metric. Requirements coverage is a coverage metric, defect density a defect metric and test execution time a test progress metric. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.1 (p. 54); FL-5.3.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: In the test pyramid, how do tests in higher layers compare with those in lower layers?

options.text: More granular and needed in larger numbers
Equally granular but with fewer assertions
More isolated, more granular and faster to run
Less granular, less isolated and slower to execute

questions.explanation: The higher the layer, the lower the test granularity and isolation and the higher the execution time, so fewer high-level end-to-end tests are needed. Lower layers contain many small, isolated, fast tests. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.6 (p. 50); FL-5.1.6 (K1).

questions.prompt: Risk likelihood is the probability that a risk occurs. Which values can it take?

options.text: Greater than zero and less than one
Any positive whole number
Any value from minus one to one
From zero to one inclusive

questions.explanation: Risk likelihood is the probability of the risk occurring and is greater than zero and less than one: an event with probability zero poses no risk, and an event that is certain to occur is a fact rather than a risk. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.1 (p. 52); FL-5.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: In agile development, what are the entry criteria that a user story must fulfil before development and testing start often called?

options.text: Definition of Ready
Acceptance criteria
Exit criteria
Definition of Done

questions.explanation: Entry criteria that a user story must fulfil before development and/or testing start are called the Definition of Ready, and exit criteria for a releasable item are often called the Definition of Done. Acceptance criteria are conditions for accepting the story. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.3 (p. 49); FL-5.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO typical entry criteria for system testing.

options.text: The number of unresolved defects is below target
All smoke tests on the build have passed
The planned coverage level has been achieved
The test environment and test data are available
All regression tests have been automated

questions.explanation: Entry criteria include the availability of resources such as environments and test data, the availability of testware, and an initial quality level such as passed smoke tests. Achieved coverage, automated regression tests and unresolved defect counts are typical exit criteria. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.3 (p. 49); FL-5.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO items that are typical content of a test plan.

options.text: Lessons learned at test completion
Actual results of each executed test
Entry and exit criteria for each test level
The risk register for product and project risks
Defect reports raised during execution

questions.explanation: Typical test plan content includes the context of testing, assumptions and constraints, stakeholders, communication, the risk register, the test approach with its entry and exit criteria, and budget and schedule.
