Actual results and defect reports come from execution, and lessons learned belong to test completion. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.1 (p. 48); FL-5.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: In which testing quadrant does the syllabus place smoke tests?

options.text: Q3: business facing, critique the product
Q4: technology facing, critique the product
Q2: business facing, support the team
Q1: technology facing, support the team

questions.explanation: Quadrant Q4, technology facing and critiquing the product, contains smoke tests and non-functional tests other than usability, which are often automated. Q1 holds component and component integration tests, Q2 functional tests and examples, and Q3 exploratory, usability and user acceptance testing. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.7 (p. 51); FL-5.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team writes API tests and simulations that check acceptance criteria while a feature is being developed. Which quadrant fits these tests?

options.text: Q4
Q3
Q2
Q1

questions.explanation: Q2, business facing and supporting the team, contains functional tests, examples, user story tests, user experience prototypes, API testing and simulations that check acceptance criteria. Q1 contains component tests, Q3 user-oriented critique and Q4 technology-facing critique. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.7 (p. 51); FL-5.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO kinds of testing that belong to quadrant Q3 (business facing, critique the product).

options.text: API testing
Component integration testing
User acceptance testing
Usability testing
Performance testing

questions.explanation: Q3 contains exploratory testing, usability testing and user acceptance testing, which are user-oriented and often manual. Component integration tests belong to Q1, API tests to Q2 and performance tests to Q4. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.7 (p. 51); FL-5.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: A company buys insurance against losses caused by failures of a new payment feature. Which response to product risk is this?

options.text: Risk acceptance
Contingency plan
Risk mitigation
Risk transfer

questions.explanation: Shifting the financial consequences to an insurer transfers the risk. Mitigation reduces the risk level, for example through testing; acceptance takes the risk knowingly; and a contingency plan prepares actions for when the risk occurs. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.4 (p. 53); FL-5.2.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a project risk rather than a product risk?

options.text: Security vulnerabilities in login
Scope creep in the requirements
Poor user experience in checkout
Inefficient algorithms in the search

questions.explanation: Scope creep is a technical issue among project risks, which affect schedule, budget or scope. Inefficient algorithms, poor user experience and security vulnerabilities relate to product quality characteristics and are product risks. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.2 (p. 52); FL-5.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Product risk analysis rates the payment module as the highest risk. Which use of this result is consistent with the syllabus?

options.text: Postponing payment tests until the final iteration
Reducing reviews because testing will find the defects
Choosing more rigorous techniques and higher coverage there
Assigning equal effort to all modules for fairness

questions.explanation: Product risk analysis results determine test scope, levels, types, techniques, coverage, effort and priority, so the highest-risk area gets more rigorous techniques and higher coverage and is tested early. Reducing reviews, equal effort and postponement ignore the analysis. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.3 (p. 52); FL-5.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which item typically appears in a test progress report and is absent from a test completion report?

options.text: Unmitigated risks and defects not fixed
Lessons learned that are relevant to testing
Testing planned for the next period
Final evaluation against the exit criteria

questions.explanation: Progress reports support ongoing control and include the testing period, progress, impediments, metrics, new and changed risks, and testing planned for the next period. Lessons learned, the final evaluation against exit criteria, and unmitigated risks with unfixed defects belong to the completion report. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.2 (p. 54); FL-5.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: How does test reporting within the team typically differ from test completion reporting?

options.text: It omits test metrics and impediments
It is written for external auditors alone
It is produced once, using a set template
It is frequent and informal rather than templated

questions.explanation: Test progress reporting to others in the same team is often frequent and informal, while test completion reporting follows a set template and occurs once. Different audiences need different information, formality and frequency. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.2 (p. 54); FL-5.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A test team is distributed across three time zones. Which way of communicating test status is most appropriate?

options.text: No status communication until test completion
Identical detailed logs for every stakeholder
Verbal updates at a daily meeting in one office
More formal communication, such as written reports

questions.explanation: More formal communication may be more appropriate for distributed teams, where direct face-to-face communication is not always possible because of distance or time differences. Office-only verbal updates exclude remote members, and communication should be ongoing and tailored to stakeholders. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.3 (p. 55); FL-5.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A test environment has been approved for testing and has become a baseline. How can it be changed afterwards?

options.text: It can never be changed after approval
Only through a formal change control process
By any tester who needs a different setting
By replacing it with the newest component versions

questions.explanation: Once a configuration item is approved for testing it becomes a baseline and can only be changed through a formal change control process. Uncontrolled edits or silently taking newer versions break reproducibility, and baselines can change, just not informally. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.4 (p. 56); FL-5.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A defect report states that a failure occurred on last month's build. How does configuration management help the team investigate it?

options.text: It removes the need to record the test environment
It ensures that later builds behave identically
It allows reverting to a previous baseline to reproduce results
It replaces the defect workflow with version numbers

questions.explanation: Configuration management records changed items when a new baseline is created, making it possible to revert to a previous baseline and reproduce earlier test results. It still requires environments to be recorded, does not make builds behave identically, and complements defect management. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.4 (p. 56); FL-5.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: What does configuration management ensure in order to support testing?

options.text: Test cases are executed in order of their risk
Items are uniquely identified and version controlled
Results are reported to stakeholders daily
Defects are fixed before each new baseline

questions.explanation: Configuration management ensures that configuration items, including test items, are uniquely identified, version controlled, tracked for changes and related for traceability, and that testware references them unambiguously. Prioritization, defect fixing and daily reporting are other activities. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.4 (p. 56); FL-5.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: In a comparable previous project, the development-to-test effort ratio was 5:2. Development effort for the new project is estimated at 750 person-days. Using estimation based on ratios, what is the test effort estimate?

options.text: 300 person-days
1875 person-days
450 person-days
375 person-days

questions.explanation: With a development-to-test ratio of 5:2, test effort is 2/5 of development effort: 750 × 2 / 5 = 300 person-days. 1875 inverts the ratio, 450 uses 3/5 and 375 halves the development effort. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: Test effort in the last three iterations was 24, 30 and 33 person-days. The team extrapolates the next iteration as the average of the last three. What is the estimate?

options.text: 33 person-days
30 person-days
29 person-days
87 person-days

questions.explanation: Extrapolating as the average of the last three iterations gives (24 + 30 + 33) / 3 = 29 person-days. 33 uses only the latest value, 30 is the median and 87 the total. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: Experts estimate a test task as a = 4, m = 10 and b = 22 person-hours. Using three-point estimation with E = (a + 4m + b) / 6 and SD = (b − a) / 6, what is the estimate?

options.text: 11 ± 3 person-hours
10 ± 3 person-hours
11 ± 18 person-hours
12 ± 3 person-hours

questions.explanation: E = (4 + 4 × 10 + 22) / 6 = 66 / 6 = 11 and SD = (22 − 4) / 6 = 3, so the estimate is 11 ± 3 person-hours, that is 8 to 14. 10 is only the most likely value, 12 is the simple average of the three estimates, and 18 is b − a without dividing by 6. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: In a Wideband Delphi estimation, three experts estimate 8, 9 and 20 days. The agreed boundary requires every estimate to lie within 25% of the median. What happens next?

options.text: The most experienced expert chooses the value
The average of 12.3 days becomes the estimate
The experts discuss, then each re-estimates in isolation
The highest estimate is accepted to be safe

questions.explanation: The median is 9 days, so 20 lies outside the agreed boundary of 6.75 to 11.25 days. In Wideband Delphi the experts then discuss their estimates and each makes a new estimate in isolation, repeating until consensus. Averaging, deferring to one expert or taking the maximum skips this feedback cycle. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt:
Test cases cover these requirements:
T1: R1, R2
T2: R2, R3, R4
T3: R1, R5
T4: R4
T5: R3, R4
Using additional coverage prioritization, which test case is executed second?

options.text: T1
T4
T5
T3

questions.explanation: T2 covers the most requirements (R2, R3, R4) and runs first. Additional coverage then counts only uncovered items: T3 adds R1 and R5, T1 adds R1, and T4 and T5 add nothing. T3 is therefore second, although T5 has the same total coverage as T3. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: Test cases have these risk-based priorities: TC1 high, TC2 medium, TC3 high, TC4 low. TC3 needs a test environment that is available on day 2 alone; the others can run on day 1. Each day, all available test cases run in priority order. What is the execution order?

options.text: TC1, TC3, TC2, TC4
TC1, TC2, TC3, TC4
TC3, TC1, TC2, TC4
TC1, TC2, TC4, TC3

questions.explanation: On day 1 the available test cases run by priority: TC1 (high), TC2 (medium), TC4 (low). TC3 has high priority, but its environment is available only on day 2, so it runs last. The execution order must take the availability of resources into account. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt:
Statements covered by each test case:
T1: S1, S2, S3, S4
T2: S3, S4, S5, S6, S7, S8
T3: S1, S9
T4: S2, S10, S11
Using additional coverage prioritization, what is the execution order?
questions.explanation: T2 covers six statements and runs first. Of the uncovered S1, S2, S9, S10 and S11, T4 adds three, then T3 adds S1 and S9, and finally T1 adds nothing new. Ordering by total coverage instead would give T2, T1, T4, T3. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: In release 3.2, applying voucher SAVE10 to a cart totalling 80.00 shows 88.00 where 72.00 is expected. Which defect report title is best?

options.text: Voucher SAVE10 raises cart total instead of reducing it
Voucher code contains a sign error in the discount calculation
Voucher SAVE10 does not work for some customers
Critical: vouchers must be fixed before the 3.2 release

questions.explanation: A title should give a short summary of the anomaly: what happens under which conditions. The vague title does not identify the anomaly, the sign-error title states an unverified cause, and the critical title expresses priority instead of describing the failure. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A defect report contains a unique ID, title, date and author, test object and environment, context with the test case and data, steps to reproduce with logs, actual result, severity, priority, status and a reference to the test case. Which essential element is missing?

options.text: The expected result
A summary of other test results
A proposed root cause
The configuration management plan

questions.explanation: A defect report should include both expected and actual results so readers can see why the behavior is an anomaly. A proposed cause is not required and may be wrong, and summaries of other results and configuration management plans are not defect report contents. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A developer fixes a reported defect and deploys the fix to the test environment. Which status should the defect report now have?

options.text: Deferred to a later release
Awaiting confirmation testing
Re-opened for further analysis
Closed as resolved by the developer

questions.explanation: After a fix is deployed, the report waits for confirmation testing, and it is closed only when that test passes. Deferred means that the fix is postponed, and re-opening applies when a confirmation test fails. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: Analysis of a reported anomaly shows that the test's expected result was wrong and the software behaves correctly. How should the report be handled?

options.text: Reopen it as a high-severity defect
Defer it to the next planned release
Reject it as a false positive and fix the test
Close it as fixed after a confirmation test

questions.explanation: Reported anomalies may turn out to be something other than defects, such as false-positive results, and the workflow decides a suitable response: here, rejecting the report and correcting the test. Closing as fixed, deferring or reopening treats it as a real product defect. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team uses containers to create identical test environments on demand for every pipeline run. To which tool category does this belong?

options.text: Scalability and deployment standardization tools
Test execution and test coverage tools
Non-functional testing tools for load and stress
Test design and test implementation tools

questions.explanation: Virtual machines and containerization tools support scalability and deployment standardization. Test design and implementation tools generate cases, data and procedures, execution and coverage tools run tests and measure coverage, and non-functional tools test characteristics such as performance under load. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.1 (p. 59); FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tool generates test data and test procedures from a model of the system. Which category of test tool is this?

options.text: Test design and test implementation tools
Test execution and coverage tools
Test management tools for tracking tests
DevOps tools for build pipelines

questions.explanation: Test design and implementation tools facilitate the generation of test cases, test data and test procedures. Management tools track tests, defects and requirements, DevOps tools support the delivery pipeline, and execution tools run tests and measure coverage. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.1 (p. 59); FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team uses a spreadsheet to record test conditions and their status. How does the syllabus classify the spreadsheet?

options.text: As a test execution tool
As a static analysis tool for documents
As no tool at all, since it is office software
As a test tool, because it assists in testing

questions.explanation: Any tool that assists in testing is a test tool; the syllabus notes that a spreadsheet is a test tool in the context of testing. It does not analyze work products statically or execute tests. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.1 (p. 59); FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which tool category supports the delivery pipeline, workflow tracking, automated builds and CI/CD?

options.text: DevOps tools
Test management tools
Static testing tools
Collaboration tools

questions.explanation: DevOps tools support the DevOps delivery pipeline, workflow tracking, automated build processes and CI/CD. Collaboration tools facilitate communication, test management tools manage tests and defects, and static testing tools support reviews and static analysis. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.1 (p. 59); FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which is a potential benefit of test automation?

options.text: Independence from the tool vendor's support
More objective assessment, such as coverage
Replacement of critical thinking by testers
No need for maintenance of test scripts

questions.explanation: Automation can provide more objective assessment, such as coverage, and measures too complicated for humans to determine. Scripts still need maintenance, dependency on a vendor is a risk, and relying on a tool instead of critical thinking is a risk. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.2 (p. 59); FL-6.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which is a risk of using an open-source test tool?

options.text: It cannot be used for regression testing
It costs more than comparable commercial tools
It removes the need to train the testers
It may be abandoned and receive no further updates

questions.explanation: A listed risk is that open-source software may be abandoned, so no further updates are available, or that its components need frequent updates. Higher cost, unsuitability for regression testing and removing the need for training are not risks the syllabus names. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.2 (p. 59); FL-6.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Select TWO potential risks of test automation.

options.text: A tool that breaches regulatory or safety standards
Reduced test execution times and faster feedback
Easier access to statistics about test progress
A tool incompatible with the development platform
More time for testers to design deeper tests

questions.explanation: Risks include an automation tool that is not compatible with the development platform and choosing an unsuitable tool that does not comply with regulatory requirements or safety standards. Faster feedback, easier access to test information and more time for deeper tests are benefits. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.2 (p. 59); FL-6.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which is a potential benefit of test automation for test management and reporting?

options.text: Elimination of manual testing
Easier access to test progress statistics
Removal of the need for a test plan
Automatic acceptance of residual risks

questions.explanation: Automation gives easier access to information that supports test management and reporting, such as statistics, graphs and aggregated data about progress, failure rates and execution duration. It does not replace planning, decide on risk acceptance or remove the need for manual testing. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.2 (p. 59); FL-6.2.1 (K1).
